[P2] The "cannot delete the active account" guard reads `m.active` here, before `acquireMutation` (line 97), and never re-checks after acquiring the token. A switch A->X holds the mutation token for its whole duration and only sets active=X at commit. Sequence: active=A; a client calls delete X while X is inactive (guard passes) and blocks on the token held by the in-flight switch; the switch commits (active=X) and releases the token; deleteAccount then proceeds and removes X's descriptor and vault credential -- the now-active account. `logout` in this file does it correctly (reads active after acquiring the exclusive lease + token). [P2] `RecoverClaudeCodeCredentialSwitch` calls `txn.Rollback` here with no defer to release the native credential locks. `Rollback` acquires both native locks but only releases them (ReleaseNativeLocks) after `keychain.Set` and `WriteOAuthAccount` both succeed; if either fails it returns before that release, and this method has no defer to clean up. Because a heartbeat keeps the lock directory's mtime fresh, it never ages past the stale threshold, so every future Claude credential switch deadlocks until the daemon restarts. The normal worker (`runClaudeCodeAccountSwitch`) has `defer txn.ReleaseNativeLocks()`; this recovery caller is missing it. Add a defer release regardless of Rollback's result.

[P1] Reset the active pointer when recovery restores the source

The source and default recovery branches restore account A's canonical credential/config and then return `RecoveryFailed`, but they never reconcile an active pointer that may already have advanced to B. If the pointer commit succeeded but the final durable phase did not, and recovery classifies the canonical credential as source/unknown (including after the unlocked verification race), this leaves pointer=B while credential/config=A; marking the switch failed makes that split-brain state terminal. CAS the pointer back to the source when rollback wins, or retain `recovery_required` until pointer and credential agree.

[P1] Fence the final credential verification and pointer CAS

The native Claude locks are released before `VerifyGlobal` and `CommitActivePointer`. A native Claude process can therefore replace the keychain credential/config in this gap. `VerifyGlobal` only proves that some credential is logged in and that the config UUID names the target; it never proves the canonical credential belongs to that target. Keep the locks, or reacquire them after the CLI probe and re-check both the normalized target credential and identity before performing the CAS.

[P1] Do not require POSIX directory fsync on Windows

Every journal write opens the directory with `"r"` and then calls `sync()`. On Windows, libuv implements fsync with `FlushFileBuffers`; that API requires write access, while this handle has only read access. The directory flush therefore fails after the rename. `ensureStagedJournal()` treats even its initial empty-journal write as a restore failure, and subsequent writes keep setting `journalPersistenceError`, so `quitAndInstallUpdate()` remains blocked for Windows users.

Use a platform-supported durability strategy instead of treating an unsupported directory flush as a failed journal transaction. I exercised the post-rename access-denied path with fault injection; this was not a native Windows run. The access requirement is documented by [Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-flushfilebuffers), and the implementation is in [libuv](https://github.com/libuv/libuv/blob/v1.48.0/src/win/fs.c#L1950).

[P1] Preserve A across native errors after the ZIP transfer resolves

The awaited MacUpdater download promise is resolved by the proxy response's `finish` event, which only proves the ZIP was sent. Native validation can still reject B afterwards. This transition has already deleted A and changed the journal to `native-possibly-staged(B)`, so the later `error` handler no longer takes its replacement-failed branch and the install guard permits `quitAndInstall()`.

I reproduced this using the installed MacUpdater's real `updateDownloaded()` method and a loopback ZIP request, followed by a native error: the durable record still names B, A is absent, and AO permits installation. MacUpdater also retains its `squirrelDownloadedUpdate` flag from A, so the explicit quit path cannot be assumed to wait for B. Keep the uncertainty/provenance and install guard until the relevant native completion is known, or retain a conservative A/B record when that boundary cannot be established. The documented exclusion of atomic native replacement does not make dropping the warning at HTTP completion safe.

Cancel/rebase dependent queued transitions on failure, or commit live and durable state coherently; a later snapshot must not silently clear the safety barrier while live state remains rolled back.

After A is staged on Stable, discover B on Nightly and let B fail. Switching back to Stable returns A here and exits before reconciling the failed B replacement. The journal remains `replacement-failed(A,B)` and the UI keeps offering Retry B even though the selected channel now offers A. `cliMissing` cannot distinguish "gh is absent" from "we don't know yet."

**Blocking safety gap (AC-10/AC-18/AC-22): TUI automation bypasses the automation guard at the just-in-time write boundary.** Only Chat is re-read above with `NeedsInput`; TUI falls through to `m.send`, which uses `sessionguard.DeliverWithPostWrite`. `Deliver` intentionally permits `waiting_input` and active sessions because it is the user-send policy, while automation must refuse waiting-input and must not write mid-turn unless explicitly safe. A destination can change idle→waiting_input/active after `Dispatcher.destination` and before this write. Route TUI through an automation-specific guarded primitive that rechecks waiting/blocked/startup/input-gate/active at the pane write and verifies the harness can emit the exact acknowledgement; unsupported TUI harnesses must fail closed without a write. **Blocking semantic/re-arm gap (AC-1/AC-3): this duplicates and weakens AO's canonical readiness rule.** It treats `unstable` as ready and omits unresolved human review threads, while `scmObservationIsReadyToMerge`/`domain.MergeReadiness.ReadyToMerge` requires computed `mergeable` and no unresolved comments. The orchestrator can therefore receive `worker_ready_to_merge` when AO's own notification/read model says it is not ready. Also the terminal `o.Merged || o.Closed` branch never records this source false, so ready→closed→reopened-ready cannot re-arm. Derive from the canonical SCM readiness projection and clear the source on every non-ready observation, including terminal ones; test comments, unstable/unknown, close/reopen, and repeated observations.

**Blocking durability/re-arm gap (AC-3/AC-4): termination and outbox enqueue are separate operations, and not all terminal paths call this helper.** `MarkTerminated` commits the session mutation and only then calls this method, leaving a crash window with a durable terminated fact and no event or startup reconstruction. `ApplyRuntimeObservation`'s reaper-driven termination does not call it at all. Finally source `session` is only ever set active=true; restore never clears it, so terminate→restore→terminate emits once. Make the terminal fact/outbox atomic or startup-reconcilable across every terminal path and persist a recurrence generation/re-arm on restore. Add real-store fault tests for commit-before-event, reaper death, daemon restart, and terminate/restore/terminate.

**Blocking operability gap (AC-14/AC-15/AC-19): `attention_required_at` is not a durable human-visible alert.** Nothing creates a notification, emits CDC for this table, or renders this state in desktop/mobile; the only consumer is a new list endpoint that an operator must already know to poll, and that endpoint only returns the newest 100 rows. **Security gap (AC-17/AC-19): control-character stripping and truncation do not redact credentials.** Transport/provider errors can contain credential-bearing URLs, bearer/token fragments, environment values, or provider response text; this function persists that verbatim in `last_error` and exposes it through the API. Store a typed safe error code/classification or use the project's credential/URL redactor, and test representative bearer tokens, query credentials, API-key-shaped values, newlines/ANSI, and length bounds. The current test's literal word `secret` demonstrates it remains rather than asserting redaction.

**Acknowledgement race (AC-4/AC-12): a TUI prompt-submit hook may acknowledge the leased batch before `Submit` returns.** This unconditional `Mark...Submitted` then requires `state='leased'`; if the hook already changed it to `acknowledged`, the state fence fails and a successful delivery is reported as dispatch failure. This is especially likely for harnesses whose send path waits for an active hook. Make submitted marking idempotent for an already-acknowledged matching token (without weakening the token/destination fence), and add a test where the transport invokes exact acknowledgement synchronously before returning.

Replayed scrollback arms the CPR correlator, so historical DSRs get answered into the live PTY.

`handle.write` is also the path `useTerminalSession` uses to replay scrollback on attach/reattach (`terminal.write(replay)` / `writeReplayBatches`). Any `\x1b[6n` recorded in the history — zsh/bash prompts and most TUIs probe cursor position routinely — increments `pendingReports` here; xterm re-parses the DSR while replaying, emits a CPR on `onData`, and `push` sees `pendingReports > 0` and forwards `\x1b[7;21R` to the **live** PTY. $ HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 gh auth status  ; echo $?   # 1

Traced path on reattach:

1. scrollback is written through `handle.write` (`useTerminalSession.ts:454`, `:471`, `:555`)
2. `observeOutput` counts any historical `\x1b[6n` into `pendingReports` (`osc-color-report.ts:154`)
3. xterm re-parses the replay and generates a CPR
4. `term.onData` -> `push()` sees `pendingReports > 0` and emits (`osc-color-report.ts:171-173`)
5. `emitUserInput(report, "protocol")` (`XtermTerminal.tsx:1002`), which has no visibility or ownership gate

So reattaching to a pane whose scrollback contains a DSR writes a stray `^[[r;cR` into the running process. p10k prompts and agent TUIs emit cursor-position queries routinely, so the trigger is ordinary. Both failure modes live on the same path, which is why the branch has now flipped between them twice. Two fixes that avoid a mux protocol change:

1. **Split the counter.** Track replay-originated credits separately from live ones; `push()` consumes replay credits first and discards those reports, then consumes live credits and emits. Ordering is safe because xterm parses writes in order.
2. **Discriminate on the handle, not the write.** The renderer already knows whether it just created the terminal or is reattaching. A brand-new PTY has no history (cover window all live); a reattach's cover window is all history. That's the distinction actually needed, and it's available at the call site.

**Caveat on my confidence:** this is static analysis. I have not confirmed empirically that the replay buffer retains `\x1b[6n` verbatim, nor that xterm re-emits on re-parse — though the deleted `dispose()` suggests the original author believed both.

Rather than applying a fix on my say-so, the cheap way to settle it is the mirror of the test just added: seed a session's scrollback with `\x1b[6n`, reattach, and assert nothing reaches the PTY. If nothing is emitted this is closed and I'm wrong. If a `^[[r;cR` appears, it's confirmed and that test is exactly what should guard the fix. Given the branch has cycled between both failure modes, pinning both directions with tests is what stops it recurring.

`ClearAll` deletes shared durable state but never publishes a clear or invalidation event. Only the QueryClient that issued the DELETE is reset. Publish an ordered clear event and have each client clear or refetch its cache.

**[P1] Keep the fresh-stream snapshot from overwriting a newer event**

Each reset opens a new EventSource, and its `onopen` invalidates both active history queries. The GET can read the empty post-clear table, then a new notification can be inserted and delivered on the fresh stream, and finally the older GET response can resolve and replace the cache with its empty page. The stream stays healthy, so that notification and its badge can remain missing until an unrelated refetch. The new test dispatches on `freshSource` without firing `onopen`, so it does not cover this sequence. The backend publishes `notification_cleared` before the DELETE handler writes its response, then releases the shared barrier. This unconditional cache clear and badge reset then erase that legitimate post-clear notification. The stream stays healthy, so nothing restores it until an unrelated refetch. Every buffered event is applied immediately at receipt and again here. `created` merges are idempotent, but `applyResolvedNotification` always subtracts one from `unresolvedCount`. If a cache was inactive and not replaced by the snapshot, or if the snapshot already included the resolution, this replay subtracts a second time. The recent-history query is inactive whenever the panel is closed, so one resolution during an unread reconnect snapshot can undercount unrelated unresolved notifications. An in-flight command that is mid-`respond()` when `cancelConnectionCommands` fires can get two cancellation results:

1. `cancelConnectionCommands` iterates `activeCommands` and calls `sendCancelledResultOnTarget` (synchronous write) for the command
2. The `controller.abort()` on the next line causes `respond()`'s catch to call `sendCancelledResult` (async send) for the same `requestId`

The `activeCommands.delete(command.requestId)` in the `finally` block runs after the catch, so the command is still in `activeCommands` when the synchronous loop writes the first frame. The daemon broker sees two result frames for the same `requestId`.

If you want belt-and-suspenders, check `activeCommands.has(command.requestId)` before the async send, or just delete from `activeCommands` before aborting controllers in `cancelConnectionCommands`.

Same by-cause concern as the `destroy` path, plus a semantic one specific to the force path: `forceDestroyPath` and `ForceDestroy` are also driven from spawn rollback and discard flows, whose callers don't participate in the `Cleanup` retry loop. Because the sentinel is applied to every `removeAllWithRetry` failure, this fixed string is shown even when nothing is holding the directory (a permission or mount failure). `repoTeardownLock` keys the map on whatever repo string the caller passes, but the callers do not agree on its form. `destroy` and `ForceDestroy` resolve the repo through `repoPathForInfo` -> `physicalAbs` (`filepath.Abs` + `Clean` + `EvalSymlinks`), while `forceDestroyPath` locks on its raw `repo` argument, which `DestroyWorkspaceProject` fills directly from `WorkspaceProjectInfo.Worktrees[].RepoPath`. If a worktree row carries a repo path that is not already symlink-resolved and absolute (a relative path, a trailing slash, or a symlinked parent), it maps to a different key than the `physicalAbs` form the destroy path uses. The two then take different locks and their `git worktree remove`/`prune`/`list` commands run against the same physical repo at once, which is the interleaving this lock is meant to prevent.

Canonicalize the key in one place: run `physicalAbs` on `repo` inside `repoTeardownLock` (or before every call) so all three entry points land on the same mutex regardless of what the caller passed.

**[P1] Bound favicon downloads before buffering them**

This new suggestion path automatically starts up to four favicon fetches, but `fetchFaviconFromSession` calls `response.arrayBuffer()` before checking `MAX_FAVICON_BYTES`. A large or never-ending `/favicon.ico` can therefore consume unbounded memory or leave work hanging in Electron's main process merely when a matching history suggestion appears. Please enforce the limit while streaming (and reject an oversized `Content-Length` when available), cancel above the limit, and add a request timeout.

**[P2] Keep suggestion favicon requests inside the selected browser profile**

Initializing `favicon` to `${origin}/favicon.ico` makes the shell renderer request every uncached suggestion directly, while `historyFavicon` independently fetches the same URL through the isolated browser session. This duplicates requests and bypasses the selected profile's cookie/proxy/session boundary, leaking imported-history origins through the shell session. Please render the cached tab icon or placeholder until the profile-session IPC returns a data URL; reserve direct URLs for a preview mode where that IPC is unavailable.

**[P2] Prevent late history results from reopening after Escape**

Escape clears the current suggestions, but it does not invalidate the active debounce or IPC request. If that request resolves afterward, its callback repopulates `historySuggestions` and reopens the menu despite the user's dismissal. Please invalidate pending requests with a generation token or track an explicit dismissed state until the input changes/refocuses, and add a deferred-promise regression test.

Fixed in 2eb610215: favicon responses now reject oversized Content-Length values before reading, stream through a 256 KiB hard cap with cancellation, and use a 5-second AbortController timeout. Added coverage for declared oversize, streamed oversize, and stalled requests.

Fixed in eebd384bf: native Electron suggestions now render a cached icon or placeholder until the selected browser profile IPC returns a data URL. Direct favicon URLs are restricted to non-native preview mode, eliminating duplicate shell-session requests and preserving the profile cookie/proxy/session boundary.

Fixed in bb8a7349b: history lookups now carry a generation token that is invalidated immediately on Escape, input changes, blur, navigation, page focus, and popover dismissal. Added a deferred-promise regression test proving a response resolved after Escape cannot reopen the menu.

[P1] Track the newly completed response instead of rescanning all history

After the initial snapshot, `isInitialSnapshot` is always false, but this loop still starts at the first transcript item. For a session whose history contains an old assistant URL before the latest user turn, the next snapshot change (including completion of the current response or an unrelated refresh) opens that old URL and then adds the session to `autoOpenedLinkSessions`, preventing the new response link from ever opening. I reproduced this with an initial `[old assistant URL, current user message]` snapshot followed by a capability-only snapshot update; `openInBrowser` was called with the old URL. Keep a per-session sequence/revision baseline and only inspect assistant messages that newly transitioned to complete.

This completion targets `activeEntry(browserSession)`, not the tab/page that originally submitted the batch. If tab A submits, the user switches to annotated tab B while the send request is in flight, and the request then succeeds, this deletes B’s unsent annotation session while leaving A’s already-sent session intact (so it can reappear and be resent). Please carry the submitting tab ID and page key/token through the completion payload and clear that exact stored session.

If `copyFile` fails here, the previous sound is already gone (loop above) while `ui-settings.json` still points at the old path — so a failed re-pick leaves the user with neither file nor a coherent setting.

Safer pattern: copy to a temp name first (or only delete other entries after this copy succeeds).

This caches `null` as well as successful payloads. A one-off read failure (file briefly locked/missing) then sticks for the rest of the session until Test / path change / restart.

I'd only cache a non-null payload (or clear on null so the next notification retries).

`silent` is keyed off `notificationSoundPath !== null`, not off whether custom audio actually plays. Combined with `playNotificationSound` returning after `shell_.send(...)` with no ack, a missing file or a renderer that hasn't registered `onPlay` yet can yield a silent toast and no custom sound (beep only if you hit the fallback branch).

Consider setting `silent` only when you're about to send a real payload — or always keep beep as backup when send can't be confirmed.

Defense in depth: this will read any path with a supported extension. `uiSettings:set` can also persist an arbitrary `notificationSoundPath`. Happy path only writes under `notification-sound/`, but nothing enforces that on read.

Worth rejecting paths outside `<stateDir>/notification-sound/` (and ideally ignoring path writes via `uiSettings:set` so only choose/clear can set it).
Filename + Choose + Test + Reset on one row will get tight on narrow settings widths. Low priority, but wrapping or parking Test/Reset in a second control group would help.

Blocking: `ensureQueryData` inherits `retry: 1` from `sessionUsageQueryOptions`, so when the usage endpoint is slow or down (daemon starting, cold backend, offline), this loader holds the whole board navigation through the retry backoff before the try/catch can resolve. Reproduced locally: base commit passes the cross-platform-focus 'New task from the project menu' spec 3/3 in ~8s; with this loader it fails intermittently (1.2m runs, menuitem click times out because the board mounts late and the `.first()` Project-actions click lands on the sidebar menu). Disabling just the project loader restores 3/3 in ~6s. This matches the renderer-smoke CI failure (same spec, all 3 platforms). Suggested fix: skip the backoff for the preload only, e.g. `ensureQueryData({ ...sessionUsageQueryOptions(projectId), retry: false })`. Applied exactly that tweak in my scratch worktree and the spec went 3/3 green; the mounted `useSessionUsageSummaries` keeps `retry: 1` so its own lifecycle is unchanged. Usage stays supplementary in the worst case (board mounts immediately, badges fill in when the query resolves) instead of delaying the board for metrics.

context.WithoutCancel(ctx) removes both cancellation and the deadline. If a Start, Stop, edit, or branch operation currently holds this session gate, StopAll can now wait past the configured hard ShutdownTimeout, potentially indefinitely. That replaces the earlier skipped-close problem with an unbounded shutdown. Please keep the original deadline for contended gates while still ensuring uncontended controllers all receive a close attempt, and add a regression that pre-holds one gate, verifies another healthy controller closes, and asserts StopAll returns by the deadline.

This `delete` runs for every completed/recovered event, but the held error is only forwarded on two paths above it: turn ends `failed` with no error of its own, or more output arrives. A `turn/completed` with `status:"completed"` (or `interrupted`) after a `willRetry:false` error takes neither path, so the error is dropped silently.

Simplest fix: remove `terminalErrors` and emit the error row immediately, as before this PR. The controller's `settledTurnState` already marks the turn failed when an error is attached.

The backend only sets `reauthRequiredAt` when protocol fields say so (`codexErrorInfo:"unauthorized"`, ACP `actions:["login"]`), and `client.go` explicitly says never to match provider prose. This regex re-decides the same thing from the message and disagrees for e.g. `Unauthorized (401)`, `Authentication failed`, `OAuth token has been revoked` (all `false`), which hides the `codex login` command exactly when it is needed. The test only passes because the fixture message contains "Login".

Suggest deleting the regex: if `reauthRequiredAt` is set, show the command. If access-denied really needs different copy, have the backend send one bool rather than guessing here.

Previously guarded by `Message != ""`. `codexProviderFailure` returns a non-nil `"Provider error"` for an empty struct, and `settledTurnState` now treats any attached error as failed, so `{"status":"completed","error":{}}` becomes a failed turn. Protocol requires `message`, so low likelihood, but same applies to `history.go`.

`detail` is nil if `Unmarshal` fails or `Detail` is empty; writing to it panics. Unreachable today since `Detail` always comes from `json.Marshal`, but a one-line `if detail == nil` guard, or dropping the `superseded` marker entirely (see review body), avoids it.

Blocking: this path adopts a device credential whose identity cannot be established. A bare `{"tokens":{"access_token":"test-only"}}` parses with nil error (`ProviderAccountID == ""` is allowed), matches nothing, and is then imported as a managed account with the active pointer set — `runGlobalReconciliation` reports Verified. That is exactly what the rewritten integration test forbids (`unmatched signed-out device credential was treated as a managed account`; it expects `UnmanagedGlobalAccount` set and no active pointer). I reproduced the test failure locally. Suggested fix: in the `codexCredentialMatchNone` branch, require a distinguishable identity before importing (non-empty provider account id or API-key method); otherwise record the unmanaged state and return the unverified failure, which is also what makes the second `Ensure` assertion and the device-only recovery assertions pass. [P3] Compare canonical versions during revalidation

Discovery stores `semver.valid(metadata.version)`, but this line compares that canonical value against the raw plist string. Re-run `semver.valid(metadata.version ?? "")` here and compare the canonical values; add one normalized-version test.

[P2] Bind the validated object to the destructive operation

This closes the long confirmation-dialog race, but there is still a pathname check/use gap between `await dependencies.revalidate(copy)` and `trashItem(copy.path)`. A replacement renamed into the path after revalidation is still what gets trashed. Please make the handoff identity-bound/atomic, for example by first moving the candidate to a private unique staging path, validating the moved object there, and restoring it on mismatch, rather than validating one pathname lookup and deleting a later one. A regression test should swap the path after `revalidate` resolves.

**[P1] Preserve the recovery handle for uncertain steering.** The daemon can return `CHAT_STEER_UNCERTAIN` after the provider may already have accepted this guidance, and its recovery contract requires the original `ClientMessageID` with `recoverOnly`. This UUID exists only in this invocation and is never persisted or exposed, so rerunning the command generates a new ID and can deliver the correction twice. Please preserve or expose the handle and support same-ID recovery; the focused failure test should exercise `CHAT_STEER_UNCERTAIN`.

**[P2] Do not let the idle fallback become a queued correction.** Another turn can start after the steer request returns `CHAT_NO_ACTIVE_TURN` but before this send lands. The messages endpoint then returns `state: "queued"`, and the CLI currently accepts it unchanged—the delay this feature is meant to avoid. If the returned turn is queued, promote that exact `turnId` through the existing queued-turn steering route, or make the daemon operation atomic, and cover the state-change race.

This follows the product decision made after the original 5151 contract was written. Reconciliation performs three quick local attempts, then leaves a stable actionable state instead of retrying indefinitely. Settings open, focus or visibility, and Try again trigger a fresh attempt. This is an intentional scope decision made after the original 5151 wording. This PR is limited to account login and management, local reconciliation, and local auth.json switching. It does not stop or restart existing sessions. The simplified credential-only behavior is therefore retained.

This is an intentional architecture decision from the later account-management discussion. Device-global auth.json is now the sole authority for which account is in use; a durable DB pointer could disagree with an external Codex login or logout and recreate split-brain state. When local reconciliation is unresolved, no saved account is presented as active. We are therefore not restoring the pointer or revision admission in this PR.

This follows the later local-switch design. A safe but unmatched device credential may be replaced only after the user selects a saved account. The source bytes or expected absence and target bytes are staged first, and the commit performs an exact local compare before the atomic write; a changed third-party credential is never overwritten. Unsafe storage disables mutation. Provider or server verification is intentionally not an admission condition, so offline switching remains possible. We are retaining this behavior for the simplified PR scope.

`failed` never resets, so a single transient image-load error permanently degrades this bubble to a filename chip for the lifetime of the mounted component — no retry, no tap-to-reload.

Minor: `attempt` looks like dead state, and the `key={attempt}` it feeds appears to be a no-op.

`attempt` can only ever increment from the `Pressable`'s `onPress`, which means the retry chip must have rendered first. So the transition is always `Pressable` → `Image` — two different element types at the same position, which React unmounts and remounts regardless of key. There is no `Image` → `Image` transition where the key would do any work.

Worth noting too that a React `key` doesn't reach the native image cache: the remount re-issues the load, but if anything ever *did* cache the failure it's the URI that would need busting, not the key. So the `key` isn't buying that either.

If I'm reading the reconciliation wrong I'd rather know — but if not, dropping `attempt` and `key` leaves `onPress={() => { haptics.tap(); setFailedLoad(undefined); }}` doing the same job with one less piece of state.

Blocking: this container flips to `flexDirection: "row"` but sets no `alignItems`, and RN/Yoga default to `stretch`. `attachmentChip` (L886) has no `height` and no `alignSelf`, so any chip sharing a line with a tile stretches to the tile's cross-axis size — a 104px or 160px tall bordered box wrapped around a single line of 12px text.

Two ways to hit it, both ordinary:

1. **Mixed attachments.** `useFileAttachments.ts:68` says the composer "supports all file types except SVG," so a message carrying a screenshot plus a `.log` or `.pdf` renders one tile and one chip on the same line.
2. **A failed image beside a successful one.** The retry chip lands in the same row as the tiles that loaded.

This didn't exist before `9ac744f94` because the container was a column, where `stretch` gave chips full width — which was what you wanted there. Flipping to `row` inverted the axis that default applies to.

Fix is one property: `alignItems: "flex-start"` on `styles.attachments`, or `alignSelf: "flex-start"` on `styles.attachmentChip`. The second is more local if you'd rather not constrain the tiles.

Caveat on my confidence: I verified the styles and the Yoga default by reading, not by rendering. An all-chips message still looks correct (every item stretches to the same natural height), so it's specifically the mixed line that breaks — worth a quick look on the simulator with one image plus one text file.

This request contains only the agent ID, so the daemon evaluates global cwd/environment rather than the selected project's provider flags and credentials. [P2] Restrict ACP authentication failures to the specified code

The pinned ACP SDK defines authentication-required as `-32000`; `-32001` is not that error and can be used for another server failure. Classifying both as auth failures turns unrelated prompt errors into reauthentication state. Remove `-32001` unless there is a concrete agent-specific structured contract for it.

[P1] Resolve provider helpers using the project PATH

`exec.LookPath` runs against the daemon's environment before `invocation.Env` is applied, so an `aws` or `gcloud` executable supplied by the project PATH is never found. The custom merge below is also case-sensitive on Windows, allowing inherited `Path` to override project `PATH`. Resolve and launch with the same merged environment, using the existing platform-aware environment semantics.

[P2] Do not classify every OAuth 400 as credential rejection

OAuth token endpoints use HTTP 400 for request and configuration errors such as `invalid_scope` and malformed requests as well as credential failures. Mapping every 400 to `ErrInvalidCredential` can block a valid service account and tell the user to reauthenticate for an AO request bug. Parse the structured OAuth error and reserve invalid state for affirmative credential rejection.

[P1] Match Claude Code's provider-selection semantics

These flags are enabled by truthy values, not merely by being non-empty, so values such as `false` currently select the wrong provider. Foundry also requires `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY=1`, which is not checked here; conversely, a stale Foundry key currently selects Foundry even when that flag is off. Parse all three provider flags consistently and reject conflicting selections instead of silently preferring Bedrock.

[P1] Clear persistent reauthentication state after recovery

This callback records a rejection, but the successful-prompt path emits no corresponding recovery signal. After the user logs in and a later controller turn succeeds, `ConversationAccount.ReauthRequiredAt` therefore remains set indefinitely, contrary to issue #4937's required recovery behavior. Emit a success/recovered account update that clears the durable flag.

[P1] Do not depend on an unsupported Foundry models endpoint

Anthropic's official Foundry client explicitly does not expose a Models endpoint, while the supported Foundry API surface is deployment-based. A valid Foundry configuration will therefore fail this probe instead of returning deployable model IDs. Source deployment names from the supported configuration/catalog path rather than testing against a fabricated `/anthropic/v1/models` contract.

[P1] Validate the endpoint Claude will actually use

The Bedrock and Vertex credentials built here never copy `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL` or `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_BASE_URL` into `Credential.BaseURL`. Consequently AO can approve the default cloud endpoint while Claude launches against a custom proxy that rejects the credential, or reject credentials that are valid only at that proxy. Carry both documented overrides into the probe credential.

[P2] Redact provider-controlled rejection text before surfacing it

`Result.Detail` promises never to contain the credential, but this copies an arbitrary provider or custom-gateway error message verbatim. A gateway can echo an authorization value or other secret into UI/log-visible state. Whitelist known safe fields/messages or explicitly redact the submitted credential before storing the detail.

[P2] Preserve a successful Bedrock CLI catalog result

`validateBedrockViaCLI` intentionally returns `StateUnknown` with non-empty models because listing models does not prove invocation permission. This condition discards that useful result every time, so a direct-probe construction failure followed by successful AWS CLI discovery still falls back to static models. Accept the Bedrock result when it contains models, matching `ProviderModels` semantics, and add that regression case.

**Bug: drag state never clears on window blur.**

`useResizable` finishes the drag on `window` `blur` (removes `is-resizing-x`, releases capture), but `ResizeHandle` only clears `dragRef` on `pointerup` / `pointercancel`. If the user starts a drag and cmd-tabs away, `dragRef.current` stays set, so `sync()` short-circuits at line 107 and the grip freezes at its last position. It then ignores window resize, sidebar collapse, and inspector toggles until the next `pointerup` anywhere (mouse `pointerId` is always 1, so any click clears it).

Add `window.addEventListener("blur", endDrag)` alongside the others, mirroring the hook.

Related: these three `window` listeners are registered for the whole lifetime of every mounted handle (sidebar + inspector), so every mouse move in the app invokes two `moveDrag` closures that immediately return. `useResizable.onPointerDown` attaches its listeners inside the pointerdown and removes them in `finish`; doing the same here in `beginDrag` / `endDrag` also makes the blur handling simpler.

**This is a second drag state machine running in parallel with `useResizable` on the same pointer events.**

`useResizable.onPointerDown` seeds `startWidth` from `widthRef` (re-seeded from the painted box only when it differs by >0.5px) and freezes `usedMax` once per drag. `beginDrag` here seeds from `rect.width` and `moveDrag` re-resolves the max on every move. Whenever the two disagree (sub-pixel `rect.width` vs `widthRef`, `rangeRef` tightening mid-drag) the grip visibly detaches from the border it is supposed to sit on. It is also why both call sites now have to pass `minWidth` / `maxWidth` twice with "MUST match" comments (Sidebar.tsx:954, SessionView.tsx:410) — that is a drift hazard, not a contract.

Two simpler shapes, either of which removes `DragState`, `resolveWidth`, `effectiveMaxWidth`, the min/max props, and the window listeners:

1. Let `useResizable` be the only integrator and expose the clamped width (e.g. an `onWidthChange(px)` option, or simply let the handle read the CSS var the hook already writes on the same targets) and position the grip from that.
2. Anchor the grip in CSS to the panel edge whose width the hook already clamps (the hit strip is already an absolutely positioned child of the panel, so a child grip moves 1:1 and stops at the same limits for free). If an `overflow-hidden` ancestor clips it, `left: var(--ao-sidebar-w)` / `right: var(--inspector-w)` on a fixed element gives the same result with no JS geometry.

The shared handle now hard-codes `.center-panel-surface`, `[data-slot='sidebar-container']` and `[data-slot='inspector-container']` (here, line 101, 189, 191) via global `document.querySelector`. Both callers already hold these elements: `Sidebar` resolves the container for `getResizeTargets`, and `SessionInspectorRail` owns `panelRef` / `gapRef` and passes them to `useResizable` via `getCssTargets`. `document.querySelector` also returns the first match in the document, which is wrong if more than one shell surface is mounted (preview / nested renders).

Prefer accepting the elements from the caller (reuse the same `getCssTargets` array, or a `getPanel` prop) so the selectors live in one place.

**This regex-parses a CSS string that SessionView generated from numbers it still has.**

`SessionView.inspectorMaxWidthCss(maxPercent, chatMinWidth)` serialises `min(P%, max(300px, calc(100% - Cpx)))`; this function decodes it with three regexes and re-implements `inspectorMaxWidthPx` (SessionView.tsx:231) with a second copy of `INSPECTOR_SEPARATOR_RESERVE_PX` (line 14 vs SessionView.tsx:123). The `absMin` fallback is already out of sync (0 here vs `WORKSPACE_ABSOLUTE_MIN_PX = 300`).

The failure mode is silent: if the CSS string ever changes shape (`clamp()`, argument order, an extra term), the `min(` regex misses, `percent` is `NaN`, and line 38 returns the full split width — i.e. the exact leftmost-overshoot bug this PR fixes comes back, and the new tests won't catch it because they pin the current string format rather than the SessionView source.

Suggest moving `inspectorMaxWidthPx` + the reserve constant into this lib (or exporting them from SessionView) and passing the number directly. Even simpler: make SessionView's `maxWidth` callback compute lazily from `splitRef.current.clientWidth` instead of caching the `defaultWidth * 2` placeholder in `rangeRef`; then `useResizable`'s `max` is always correct and neither the hook nor the grip needs to introspect CSS at all.

The probe path (67–89) is unreachable for both real callers:

- Inspector container: `max-width` is the unresolved `min()` string, and the panel is always inside `#session-workspace` with `clientWidth > 0`, so line 64 resolves.

Same for `effectiveMaxWidth`'s `split.clientWidth` fallback in ResizeHandle.tsx:71–74 — it only runs when the split formula returned `null`, which requires `clientWidth <= 8`, where its own `> 0` guard mostly fails.

**[P2] Reject a present top-level JSON `null` body**

`json.Unmarshal(null, &payload)` succeeds with a zero-value struct, so this falls through with an empty session ID and invokes the worker-spawn path. Return 400 for top-level `null`; keep accepting a truly absent body or `{}`.

**This misses the case #5366 reports.**

When two same-named files change in the same turn, `rememberTurnPathHint` sets the colliding basename entry to `undefined`. `turnFileOpenPath` then falls back to the bare `workspace-test.txt` for *both* rows — which is exactly the ambiguity the issue is about.

The new tests only ever pass a single `file_change` entry, so the collision branch is never exercised. A test with two entries sharing a basename (`alpha/workspace-test.txt` + `beta/workspace-test.txt`) would fail today.

The fix belongs in `turnFileOpenPath` / `rememberTurnPathHint` — keep all candidates per basename and disambiguate against `cwd` — rather than in the display layer.

**Basename-only hint matching can now name the wrong file.**

Given a diff row `src/a.ts` plus an unrelated `<cwd>/other/a.ts` in the turn's activity, the hint matches on basename alone and the row renders `other/a.ts`.

To be fair this isn't strictly new — the click target was already wrong in that case, so arguably this just makes the label honest about an existing bug. But the user now *sees* a wrong path where they previously saw a correct basename, so it's worth handling alongside the collision fix above (same root cause: basename-keyed hints).

**No-`cwd` fallback invents a qualifier that doesn't exist in the workspace.**

With no `cwd` hint available, `workspaceRelativeOpenPath`'s `slice(-2)` fallback prefixes the label with the worktree *directory* name — e.g. `demo-1/file.txt`. `demo-1` is a worktree folder, not a workspace path segment, so the label claims a directory the user can't find.

When there's no reliable qualifier, falling back to the plain basename reads better than a fabricated one.

**`truncate` now clips the part that identifies the row.**

This span still uses `truncate` (tail ellipsis), which was fine for basenames but cuts the wrong end now that it renders full paths: `frontend/src/renderer/comp…` drops the filename entirely.

Head-truncation (`…/renderer/components/chat/ChatTimelineItems.tsx`) or `direction: rtl` on the span keeps the filename visible, which is the one segment a user scans for.

The rename drops the concrete config key from spawn errors: a bad path now fails as `read rulesFile X: ...` for both roles, where the worker path used to name `agentRulesFile`. Since `projectRulesConfig` is constructed per role in `manager.go`, threading the field name through (e.g. a `Field` string set by each caller) would keep the error pointing at the exact key the user needs to fix. Minor: when the resolved notification is not present in a cache (for example it sits on an unfetched earlier page), this early return now leaves page.unresolvedCount stale, and unlike clears there is no invalidation after a resolved event, so the stale count persists until the next fetch. The previous unconditional decrement happened to cover that case but double-counted replays, so this is a tradeoff rather than a regression. If unresolved counts feed a badge anywhere, consider decrementing when the id is absent, or invalidating once when existing is not found.

Minor: the DELETE has already committed when Publish runs, so returning an error here tells the caller the clear failed while the rows are actually gone, and other dashboards never receive the cleared event. In practice Hub.Publish always returns nil today, so this is mostly a robustness question: logging best-effort and still returning the result (or documenting the contract) would keep the response truthful.

Minor: these count increments run on every page whenever caches[name] is true, even when the row is not actually restored. Two reachable paths: (1) the cache existed but the row was not in it, so cachedPageIndex returned -1 and positions[name] is undefined, meaning pageIndex === index never matches and nothing is inserted, yet unresolvedCount still goes up for an unresolved row (for example a read but unresolved needs_input row versus the unread cache); (2) the recorded page was dropped or replaced between the optimistic delete and the rollback. The onSettled invalidation refetches and corrects it, so this is transient, but gating the increments on the insertion actually happening (or on alreadyPresent) would keep the cache self-consistent in the window before the refetch lands.

This responder only covers loosening, not tightening. The launch overlay bakes edit/bash allow rules into OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT, so OpenCode auto-allows those tools without ever sending a permission request. Switching the picker from accept-edits or auto back to default for later turns therefore never restores prompts for those tools until the process restarts. Worth either noting the limitation in this comment or narrowing the launch overlay so downgrade paths stay reversible.

Precedence note: per OpenCode docs, custom config (OPENCODE_CONFIG / OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT) is loaded between global and project config, so an opencode.json committed at the repo root inside the worktree overrides this overlay for the permission key. In such repos accept-edits and auto silently no-op. Possibly intended (repo policy wins over an orchestration overlay), but worth confirming and stating in the doc comment.

Preferring AllowAlways persists an allow rule into the OpenCode project config, which outlives both this AO session and its bypass selection. AllowOnce would match AO per-session semantics and still suppress every request. Was Always chosen to mirror the TUI flag, or to avoid repeat round-trips? If deliberate, a short comment here would help.

addressed in c4ac865a9: explicit ids are now validated against the complete provider thread listing before any mutation. ids that belong to another pr or repository are rejected with a precondition error, so the provider is never called for them.

addressed in c4ac865a9: commentIds now accept github comment node ids and map them to their owning review thread. thread ids remain accepted for compatibility, and duplicate comment/thread inputs are resolved once.

addressed in c4ac865a9: the stale full-observation write was removed. each confirmed remote resolution now uses a targeted sqlite transaction that marks the thread and all of its comments, preserving concurrent poll updates and persisting partial success immediately.

also added an active-number ambiguity guard: if the same numeric pr is active in multiple tracked repositories, the action stops with a precondition error instead of choosing the newest row. partial-provider-listing and partial-provider-failure coverage were added, and the github adapter now requires isResolved=true in the mutation payload.

This blanket rejection disables resolve-comments entirely on thread-heavy PRs. Both providers set Partial on any truncated listing: github returns Partial: true whenever a PR has more than the 50-thread first page (observer_provider.go:322), and gitlab sets it whenever doGETPaginated hits maxPaginationPages. For those PRs every call now fails with 422, including resolve-all (which previously resolved the visible window) and explicit IDs. The doc rationale only justifies rejecting IDs absent from the window: an explicit ID present in the fetched window came from the provider response for this PR ref, so its membership is proven, and requestedThreadIDs already rejects anything not found. Suggest allowing explicit IDs that resolve against a partial window, keeping the rejection for resolve-all and for unknown IDs. If the strict behavior stands, make the error message say the listing was truncated and that retrying with explicit thread IDs works, so the 422 is actionable.

addressed in 5074d4145: resolve-all still fails closed when the provider listing is truncated, but explicit ids are now allowed when they are present in that returned window. unknown ids remain rejected before any provider mutation. the error now explains that an explicit thread or comment id is required for a partial listing, and tests cover known and unknown ids.

**A hint match with no `cwd` now throws away qualification the row already had.**

If the turn has only `file_change` activities (no command, so `hints.cwd` is undefined), `workspaceRelativeOpenPath` can't strip a root and returns the basename. So a row that *already carried* its directory segments loses them:

```
row:   src/a.ts
hint:  /w/demo-1/src/a.ts
cwd:   undefined

pre-PR:  src/a.ts
post-PR: a.ts
```

The card then shows `a.ts` and `onOpenFile("a.ts")` has nothing to resolve against. The hint matched successfully and we ended up *worse* than the input.

Suggested fix: when there's no cwd anchor, prefer the row's own `normalized` over a hint-derived basename — the hint only helps once there's a root to strip.

```ts
if (matched) {
	const open = workspaceRelativeOpenPath(matched, hints.cwd);
	return open.includes("/") || !normalized.includes("/") ? open : normalized;
}
```

**Absolute paths outside the recorded `cwd` degrade to a bare basename.**

`turnPathHints` records the *first* activity's cwd (line 60), and agents routinely run a command in a subdirectory before editing elsewhere in the worktree:

```
cwd:   /w/demo-1/frontend      (from the first command activity)
file:  /w/demo-1/backend/x.ts

pre-PR:  backend/x.ts
post-PR: x.ts
```

The `startsWith(root + "/")` check fails, so we fall straight through to `fileBasename` and the row both displays and opens an unresolvable name.

The doc comment above justifies this by saying the leading segments are worktree directory rather than workspace path — true for the *worktree root*, but not for a cwd that's a subdirectory of it. Walking up from `cwd` to the worktree root (or keeping the deepest common ancestor) would preserve `backend/x.ts` here without reintroducing the `demo-1/` fabrication.

Fixed. `turnFileOpenPath` now keeps the row's own path when a matched hint would collapse to a bare basename with no cwd to strip against: `open.includes("/") || !normalized.includes("/") ? open : normalized`. So `src/a.ts` with hint `/w/demo-1/src/a.ts` and no cwd stays `src/a.ts` instead of degrading to `a.ts`. Added a test asserting exactly that.

Fixed. `workspaceRelativeOpenPath` now anchors on the deepest directory the file and the cwd share (`commonDirPrefix`) rather than requiring the file to sit under the cwd. With `cwd=/w/demo-1/frontend` and `file=/w/demo-1/backend/x.ts` it strips the shared `/w/demo-1` and keeps `backend/x.ts`, and it still never prefixes a segment that is not already in the path, so no `demo-1/` fabrication returns. Added a test for the sibling-directory case.

**`commonDirPrefix` re-collapses the repo qualifier when the agent works inside the repo — this is #5366's symptom returning.**

```
cwd:       <workspace>/alpha        (agent cd'd into the repo — routine)
candidate: <workspace>/alpha/workspace-test.txt
row:       workspace-test.txt       (bare, as the daemon stores it)

-> workspace-test.txt               (expected alpha/workspace-test.txt)
```

The deepest shared directory *is* `<workspace>/alpha`, so the `alpha/` segment gets stripped as though it were worktree root — precisely the qualifier the card is supposed to show. The `:125` guard can't rescue it, because a bare row has no `/` to preserve.

The new tests all pass only because every one of them puts `cwd` at the workspace root or in a *sibling* directory. A case with `cwd` set to `${cwd}/alpha` and a bare row would fail today.

Anchoring on the shared prefix is the right instinct for the sibling case, but it needs a floor at the workspace root so it can't eat repo segments — otherwise the more precisely the cwd is recorded, the less qualification survives.

**The ambiguity this gives up on is solvable — the real workspace file list is a couple of components away.**

Follow the click path: `onOpenFile(openPath)` -> `handleOpenFile` -> `openResolvedWorkspaceFile` -> `matchWorkspaceFilePath(rawPath, data.files)` at `SessionView.tsx:1201`. The *click* already disambiguates against the actual workspace file list. Only the *label* is stuck guessing from turn hints — which is why it has to bail out on the two-repo case.

Threading `data.files` into `TurnChangedFiles` and deriving the label with `matchWorkspaceFilePath` would resolve `workspace-test.txt` -> `alpha/workspace-test.txt` from real data, fixing both the collision case and the inline comment above, and would let this whole heuristic go away.

Worth noting the duplication is already live: `matchTurnCandidate` re-implements `matchWorkspaceFilePath`'s exact cascade (normalize -> exact -> `endsWith('/'+rel)` suffix -> unique-basename -> fall back to input), and the string it produces is then handed to the real one to be re-resolved.

**This test satisfies the letter of #5366's acceptance criteria while asserting the opposite outcome.**

The issue asks for "one repository-qualified path format" and "a multi-repository test covers duplicate filenames in different repositories." This is that test — and it asserts `workspace-test.txt`, locking in the unqualified result the issue was filed about.

The reasoning in the comment is sound in isolation: two bare rows against two candidates genuinely are indistinguishable *from turn hints alone*, and guessing would name the wrong file. But that's an argument for getting better input (see my comment on `matchTurnCandidate`), not for encoding the gap as expected behavior — a future correct fix now has to delete a passing test, which reads like a regression.

If the bail-out stays, consider renaming it to say it's a known limitation rather than desired behavior, and leaving #5366 open.

**`normalized === rel` is unreachable.**

Candidates only enter `byBase` behind `looksAbsolutePath(file.path)` (`:64`), and both callers reach `matchTurnCandidate` only *after* an absolute-path early return (`resolveTurnFilePath:73`, `turnFileOpenPath:119`) — so `rel` is always relative and an absolute candidate can never equal it, including the `C:\` and `~` forms.

The equality test is inherited from `matchWorkspaceFilePath:25-27`, where the file list really is relative and it does real work. Here it just implies a case the control flow forbids. `normalized.endsWith(`/${rel}`)` alone is sufficient.

**The doc comment above overclaims — a fabricated worktree-dir qualifier is still reachable when `cwd` is present.**

The comment promises to "never prefix a segment that is not already in the path" and to fall back to the basename "rather than inventing a qualifier," and the test is named *falls back to the basename when cwd is missing*. Both are true only for the missing-cwd path. With a cwd pointing at a sibling worktree:

```
workspaceRelativeOpenPath("<...>/worktrees/demo/demo-1/src/a.ts",
                          "<...>/worktrees/demo/demo-2")
-> demo-1/src/a.ts
```

`demo-1` is a worktree directory, exactly the fabricated segment the previous revision removed `slice(-2)` to avoid. Lower-likelihood than the cwd-in-repo case above, but the comment currently reads as a guarantee.

**Unconditional `[direction:rtl]` changes two surfaces this PR isn't about.**

`FileLocationLabel` has three call sites; `:896` and `:1310` pass no `displayPath`, so they still render bare basenames — but they now inherit head-truncation too, flipping their ellipsis from `ChatTimeline…` to `…meItems.tsx`.

Head-truncation is the right call for the full paths at `:2569`, and arguably fine for basenames, but it's an unreviewed visual change to unrelated timeline surfaces. Gating it on `displayPath` being present (or moving the rtl class to the call site that needs it) keeps the blast radius to this PR's rows.

The clear-all mutation reconciles through its own `invalidateQueries` here rather than the transport's `snapshotRefresh` machinery, so this refetch isn't buffered against concurrent live events. Sequence: `onSuccess` empties the cache and records the generation, then starts history refetch R whose server snapshot is empty. The self-clear SSE event arrives and is a no-op (same generation). A notification is then created server-side and its `notification_created` event merges into the cache. R resolves last with its pre-create snapshot and overwrites unread + all, dropping the new row until the next event or window-focus invalidate. This is the exact lost-update the transport's `snapshotRefresh` in `notifications.ts` exists to prevent; routing the post-clear reconcile through that path (or dropping this `invalidateQueries`, since `applyNotificationsCleared` plus the self-clear event already reset the cache) closes the window.

`disabled={isEmpty || clearAll.isPending}` with `isEmpty = notifications.length === 0` also disables Clear all when the history GET failed (`allQuery.isError`) while the daemon still holds a backlog, so the user can't clear rows they can't currently load. Minor, and arguably fine since there's nothing on screen to clear; flagging it as a deliberate call for you rather than a defect.

Dropped the heuristic entirely. commonDirPrefix, workspaceRelativeOpenPath, and turnFileOpenPath are gone; the label now resolves against the real session workspace file list through matchWorkspaceFilePath. There is no shared-prefix stripping left to eat the repo segment, so a cwd inside the repo no longer changes the result.

Done as suggested. TurnChangedFiles now takes the session workspace file list (useSessionWorkspaceFileList, sharing the warm summary query) and derives each label with matchWorkspaceFilePath(file.path, files). workspace-test.txt resolves to alpha/workspace-test.txt from real data, the two-repo collision resolves, and the duplicated cascade in matchTurnCandidate is gone. Label and open target are the same string by construction.

The test now seeds the workspace file list and asserts alpha/workspace-test.txt, so it matches the acceptance criteria instead of locking in the bare basename. No known-limitation bail-out remains for this case.

Removed. matchTurnCandidate is suffix-only now (endsWith("/"+rel)); the comment records why the equality was dead code: candidates are always absolute, and callers reach it only after the absolute-path early return.

workspaceRelativeOpenPath is removed, so the fabricated worktree-dir segment can no longer reach the label. resolveTurnFilePath still joins the cwd, but only for the tooltip absolute path (meant to show the full path), not the visible label or the open target.
Gated. The [direction:rtl] + text-left classes and the bdi wrapper apply only when displayPath is set, so the two basename-only call sites keep their default tail truncation.

**[P3] `error` is missing the cloud/standalone guard that `loading` has.**

Two lines down, `loading` is gated on `!isCloudProject && !isStandalone`, but `error` is driven by `projectQuery.isError` alone.

`projectQuery` is enabled when `!isCloudProject && !isStandalone`, and `isCloudProject` derives from `cloudProjects.data`, which is `undefined` until `useCloudProjectsQuery` resolves (`enabled: ready && orgId !== undefined`). So if the composer mounts with a cloud `projectId` before that query settles, the local `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}` fires and 404s. When `cloudProjects` then resolves, `isCloudProject` flips true and the query is disabled — but React Query keeps the last result, so `isError` stays true and the context panel renders a persistent `role="alert"` row with `PROJECT_NOT_FOUND` for a perfectly healthy cloud project. `canSubmit` short-circuits on `isCloudProject`, so launch still works; it's a misleading error, not a block.

Standalone is unaffected (the query never runs). Suggest mirroring the `loading` guard:


[P1] Preserve worktree permission denies in ACP

OpenCode loads `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` as the final runtime config layer. This assignment puts AO `edit: allow` or `bash: allow` in that layer, so a session worktree `opencode.json` with `edit: deny` or `bash: deny` is overridden in Chat, contrary to the new documentation and the comment above `opencodePermissionConfig`. A repository policy can therefore be silently weakened by selecting Accept edits or Auto. Keep the AO overlay below project policy, or merge it without overriding project denies, and add a test with a worktree deny.

[P1] Apply approval changes to the live ACP process

`OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` is read at ACP process startup, but this picker writes a per-turn `approvalMode`. `applyTurnSettings` only changes the local `permissionMode`; it never changes this config. A Chat started in Auto or Accept edits therefore keeps `edit` or `bash` allowed after the user selects Default or Accept edits, while a later Bypass can still be blocked by the launch-time config. Reject unsupported transitions or apply the provider policy dynamically, and cover an Auto to Default transition in a test.

[P2] Keep bypass as a true full-access policy

ACP used to emit `permission: "allow"` for bypass, which is the OpenCode top-level full-access form. Replacing it with `{"*":"allow"}` only adds a wildcard rule; a merged project or global config can still contribute a more-specific `bash` or `edit` deny. Bypass can then remain blocked even though the UI and docs promise full access. Preserve the scalar form or explicitly override all specific denies, with a test for an existing deny.

[P1] Preserve existing inline permission denies

This assignment replaces the entire user-supplied `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT.permission` object. For example, Accept edits turns `{"permission":{"webfetch":"deny"}}` into a config containing only `{"edit":"allow"}`. OpenCode defaults most unspecified permissions to allow, so a mode that promises only to relax edits can silently enable a tool the user explicitly denied. Merge only the targeted edit/bash keys while preserving unrelated rules, including the supported string and object forms, and add a regression test with an existing deny.

[P1] Keep Auto scoped to edit and shell requests

This branch selects `allow_once` for every ACP tool kind, including fetch, read, task, and other requests. That makes Chat Auto approve permissions outside the edit and bash scope defined by `opencodePermissionConfig` and the user docs, while TUI Auto still leaves those requests to OpenCode. Gate this branch to edit/delete/move/execute kinds and add a test proving a non-edit, non-shell request remains parked for approval.

[P1] Make live permission downgrades enforceable

The launch overlay already bakes edit/bash or wildcard allows into the OpenCode process, so this responder cannot cover a later change to a stricter mode: those tools stop emitting permission requests before this function runs. A session launched in the default Auto mode can accept a switch to Default while edits and shell commands remain auto-approved; initial Bypass has the same problem, and `allow_always` adds another persistent allow. Either keep ACP launch permissions unchanged and implement reversible choices through `allow_once`, or reject/restart transitions that cannot be enforced. Add a transition test that starts in Auto or Bypass and then selects Default.

[P2] Fix the reversed precedence claim

OpenCode loads `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` after project config, not before, as its [precedence documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/config/#precedence-order) states. ACP always uses that inline source, and permission-only TUI launches do too, while prompt-file TUI uses `OPENCODE_CONFIG` before the project config. A project `edit: deny` therefore loses to AO in Chat but wins in the prompt-file TUI. Align the launch paths so both surfaces behave the same, or document the actual per-surface behavior.

OpenCode's session modes *are* agents, so the picker becomes a `session/set_config_option` on `mode`: the provider enforces the choice and it applies in both directions while the session runs. This is the bug the PR is fixing, moved down one level. Trace it through `sendOnce` with comments A and B in thread T:

- poll 1: A -> `seen[T]=sig(A)`, `attempts[T]=1`; B -> mismatch, send, `seen[T]=sig(B)`, `attempts[T]=2`
- poll 2: A -> mismatch, send again, `attempts[T]=3`; B -> mismatch, but `attempts >= reviewMaxNudge`, suppressed

So the pair duplicates, then the whole thread goes permanently silent — including any genuinely new comment that lands in it later, because the budget is spent. Both symptoms from the PR description, reproduced per thread.

The common trigger is ordinary: an agent replies to a review comment via `gh` without resolving the thread, and that reply is a second unresolved non-bot comment on the same thread.

```go
id := strings.TrimSpace(comment.ID)
if id == "" {
    id = strings.TrimSpace(comment.ThreadID)
}
```

Failure sequence, single window:

1. The user clears row X. `onSuccess` confirms the delete, then `onSettled` starts history refetch R for both the unread and all caches.
2. The daemon takes R's snapshot. It contains neither X nor anything created after it.
3. Notification N is created server-side. Its `notification_created` event arrives while R is still in flight, `snapshotRefresh` is `undefined`, so N is merged into both caches immediately.
4. R resolves last and replaces both caches with its pre-N snapshot. N disappears from the panel and from the bell badge, and nothing replays it. It returns only on the next live event or a window-focus refetch.

Neither respects `maxWorkspaceFiles`.

Measured on a 10k-file scratch workspace (40 dirs x 250 files), `origin/main` vs this branch:

| call | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `ListWorkspaceTree("")` | 238µs | 21.8ms (**~90x**) |
| `ListWorkspaceTree("dir00")` | 10.4ms | 22.1ms |

Worth pinning rather than only documenting. ACP defines exactly four option kinds (`allow_once`, `allow_always`, `reject_once`, `reject_always` — `types_gen.go:3316`), so there is no distinct kind for a permanent grant: Vibe's `allow_always` and `allow_always_permanent` both arrive as kind `allow_always`, and `PermissionOption` returns the *first* match in array order. This comment is right that AO gets the session-scoped one today, but only because Vibe happens to list it first.

That makes a security-relevant distinction depend on a third party's array order. If Vibe ever reorders those two, an AO `auto` or `bypass` session silently starts selecting the permanent grant, writing a durable tool approval into the user's Vibe config that outlives the session AO scoped it to — with no error and nothing in the transcript to show it happened.

Nothing in the test suite catches a reorder either: `offered()` sets `OptionId` to the kind string, so it can never build two options sharing a kind, and no case exercises that shape.

Cheapest fix that removes the dependency: among same-kind matches, prefer the id the binding actually wants. Even a narrow version in this driver would do — wrap `StandardPermissionPolicy` and, for an `allow_always` result, re-scan `params.Options` for the exact id `allow_always` before falling back to the first match. Whatever shape you pick, a test with two `allow_always`-kinded options in each order is what makes it stay fixed.

If you would rather keep the current behavior, it is defensible — but then the comment should say AO relies on Vibe's ordering, so the next reader knows it is an assumption rather than a guarantee.

[P1] Fold the existing inline policy into every injected tier

`existing` is decoded into `config`, but the policy passed to `acpAgentPermission` comes only from `projectPermissionRules`. With `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT={"permission":{"edit":"deny","bash":"deny"}}`, `ao-accept-edits` still gets `edit: "allow"` and `ao-auto` gets `"*": "allow"`. OpenCode applies the top-level permission before the selected agent permission, so these later agent rules override both denies. The current preservation test proves only that the original object remains in the JSON, not that it remains effective. Merge `config["permission"]` into the policy in its actual last-source order, or withhold the grant, and assert that both generated tiers keep these denies.

[P1] Include every effective global policy source before adding agent grants

OpenCode `loadGlobal` reads `config.json`, `opencode.json`, and `opencode.jsonc`; this list omits `config.json`. It also omits `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` and `OPENCODE_PERMISSION`. A deny in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode/config.json` is therefore enforced by OpenCode but invisible to AO, and the injected Auto wildcard overrides it at agent level. I reproduced that exact case. OpenCode can also merge managed and remote policy, which a file scan cannot always reconstruct, so copying selected deny files is not a safe general emulation of `--auto`. Enumerate every source in provider order and conservatively withhold grants when policy is unavailable, or auto-answer only permission requests so provider denies remain authoritative. Add coverage for `config.json` and the custom env sources.

[P1] Reverse the file pair along with the directory walk

`ConfigPaths.files` calls `up({targets: ["opencode.jsonc", "opencode.json"]}).toReversed()`. Because `up` emits both targets near-to-far, reversing the entire slice yields `opencode.json` then `opencode.jsonc` within each directory. This code appends them in the opposite order. With same-directory JSON `bash: allow` and JSONC `bash: deny`, OpenCode ends on deny while AO ends on allow, so the injected Auto agent passes a command the provider policy blocks. Clear all changes from `DELETE FROM notifications` to an `UPDATE` that sets `dismissed_at`, nothing ever removes a dismissed row, and no index covers the new predicate. Every list query then walks cleared history that only grows.

The expensive shape is the ordinary one. `idx_notifications_history` is `(created_at DESC, id DESC)`, so live rows sort first and a full page is found immediately, but a page that is not full, which is the normal case when a user has a handful of live notifications or none, forces SQLite to scan the rest of the index to prove there is nothing left. Measured on 80751083 against the store's all-history page:

| dismissed rows | per page |
|---|---|
| 0 | 76us |
| 2,000 | 437us |
| 20,000 | 16.8ms |

222x at 20k and linear from there, on a path that runs on app start, on window focus, after every mutation and after every live event. The endpoint costs more than this, since `List` also runs both count queries with the same predicate.

A partial index matching the predicate fixes it outright. Adding this and re-running the same measurement gives 26us at 20,000 dismissed rows, flat as history grows:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_notifications_live_history
    ON notifications(created_at DESC, id DESC)
    WHERE dismissed_at IS NULL;
```

Worth pairing with a sweep, since a dismissed row only has to outlive its own dedupe fact. Once `resolved_at` is set it serves no purpose, so `DELETE FROM notifications WHERE dismissed_at IS NOT NULL AND resolved_at IS NOT NULL` bounds the table instead of letting it grow for the life of the install.

Keeping the row also keeps it inside the resolution machinery, which has a client-visible cost that is easy to miss.

`ResolveSessionNotificationsByType`, `ResolvePRNotificationsByType` and `ResolveStaleNeedsInputNotifications` do not filter `dismissed_at`, so they return dismissed rows, and `Manager.publishResolved` publishes a `notification_resolved` event for each. In the renderer `applyResolvedNotification` cannot find a dismissed row in either cache, returns false, and falls through to `invalidateNotifications()`, which refetches both history queries. Every condition that resolves after the user cleared it therefore costs two history fetches in every open window, for a row nobody can see. It compounds with the scan above: those are precisely the queries that get slower as dismissed history grows.

Bursts are absorbed, since the transport's coordinator collapses concurrent invalidations, so this is steady-state waste rather than a storm. `ListOpenReadyToMergeNotifications` has the same shape: dismissed ready-to-merge rows stay in the readiness re-check loop until they resolve.

Skipping the publish needs the dismissal state above the store, which `notificationFromGen` deliberately drops today. Either carry it on the record, or have the resolve calls separate the visible rows from the ones that only need `resolved_at` written.

A 404 here means the row is already gone, which is the state the user asked for, but it is handled as a failure: the row is rolled back into the list and `handleClear` puts "Could not clear notification" in the panel.

Two windows are enough. B clears a row, A's user clicks the same row's X before A sees `notification_deleted`. A's request finds the row already dismissed, since `GetNotificationForDismissal` filters `dismissed_at IS NULL`, the service returns `NOTIFICATION_NOT_FOUND`, and A's user gets a red error for a row that is correctly gone, plus a flicker as the rollback re-inserts it and the reconcile removes it again. The same happens whenever the delete event was dropped, which the hub does by design when a subscriber's buffer is full.

Both halves are already covered by tests, just not together: `TestNotificationsAPI_DeleteUnknownNotification` for the 404, and "keeps the row visible and reports a failed single clear" for what a rejected delete does to the panel. Treating 404 as success in `deleteNotification` makes the delete idempotent and matches what the user actually sees.

The comment above justifies this gate by the delayed-callback race: a same-generation signal emitted before the process-exit report can arrive after it, and must not resurrect an exited workload. TUI is safe because it still demands user-prompt-submit as proof of relaunch, and a stale pre-exit hook carries the old LaunchID and is fenced out earlier. Chat gets no equivalent proof here: any valid non-exited signal on the current generation now clears Exited, and a plain stop does not advance or clear ControllerGeneration, so a late same-generation signal would match.

What makes that safe today is that chat activity is reported in-process from the controller goroutine (Controller.reportActivity, strictly ordered, with chat.controller.stopped emitted last and Close returning only after the run loop drains), whereas TUI activity arrives over external HTTP hooks that genuinely reorder. That asymmetry is the real reason the bypass is sound, and it is invisible at this line. If chat activity delivery ever moves off the controller goroutine or gets buffered, a stale same-generation chat.turn.completed landing after the exit would silently flip a legitimately exited session back to idle. Worth a one-line comment naming that invariant so a future change to the chat signal path does not quietly reopen this.

**[P1] #1: Configured flickers to Checking on every settings poll** (confidence 100)

On the Settings harness list, a green Configured badge cannot stay settled: every 15s poll sets readinessPoll.isFetching, which forces every installed row into Checking… for the whole ensure round-trip. Because settings auth TTL is also 15s, each interval poll nearly always performs a real authentication recheck (up to the 10s auth timeout), so users repeatedly lose Configured and see Checking/Login churn instead of the stable configured state this PR promises.

**Suggested fix:** Drop readinessPoll.isFetching from readinessChecking; drive Checking only from authState?.checking or authentication.freshness === "checking" (and optionally readinessPoll.isPending && !readinessAgent for first paint). Keep Configured visible during background refetches when effectiveReadiness is ready and freshness is still fresh. Update the "refresh fails" test so in-flight coverage uses freshness "checking" or asserts post-error Login without requiring isFetching thrash.

**[P1] #5: Poll error hides Configured, shows Login** (confidence 75)

A failed or aborted settings poll sets readinessPoll.isError for the whole batch. isReady then becomes false for every installed harness even when the shared agent-readiness cache still has effectiveReadiness ready and authentication fresh, so authorized rows temporarily render the Login/Set up action instead of the green Configured badge until the next successful poll.

**Suggested fix:** Decouple display readiness from poll query error: remove `&& !readinessPoll.isError` from isReady (and avoid using readinessPoll.isError inside rowHasError for gating the Configured badge). Keep the section-level banner for readinessPollError, and only downgrade a row when merged cache observations or authState.error say auth failed. Extend HarnessSettingsSection.test to assert Configured stays visible when cache is authorized but the poll query rejects once.

**[P2] #8: Stale authorized rows show Login** (confidence 75)

Configured is gated on authentication.freshness === "fresh". When the cached observation is still authorized/ready but freshness is stale (TTL overlay, retry-delayed snapshot without treating it as checking), isReady is false and the row falls through to the Login/Set up control with the Installed subtitle removed. Users who are already signed in are prompted to log in again even though effectiveReadiness remains ready.
