Both Homebrew operations can now unlink/link the same executable concurrently, defeating the new exclusion and potentially leaving the formulas conflicting or v1 unavailable. Make the changing check and job reservation atomic with the other worker's busy check and changing reservation, or use the same harness gate for both operations. Cover overlapping request admission; the new test only starts v1 after v2 has already marked it changing.

[P2] Rebase conditional include headers when relocating a config

The rewriter copies section headers unchanged even when materialize moves their file into <session-home>/.ao-gitconfig. Git resolves an includeIf condition beginning gitdir:./ relative to the containing config file, so relocation changes which repositories match. For example, ~/.gitconfig with [includeIf "gitdir:./"] path = work.gitconfig and a separate [include] path = ~/.gitconfig-extra matches repositories under the real home before this change. The ~/ include triggers materialization, and the unchanged condition now matches only repositories under the generated .ao-gitconfig directory; the work identity silently disappears. Home-relative gitdir:~/ conditions also still see the redirected HOME. Preserve the original condition base (including gitdir/i) when copying, and add an effective-Git test where a matching conditional supplies the identity. The new test uses an intentionally nonmatching /nonexistent/ condition, so it cannot catch this. Git documents the ./ and ~/ condition bases at https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#_conditional_includes.

[P2] Apply include rebasing to the XDG global config too

Only the ~/.gitconfig source enters gitConfigRewriter. Git's other global source, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/config (or ~/.config/git/config), is still either read directly or copied verbatim by mirrorUserGitConfig. If that file contains [include] path = ~/.gitconfig-work and that target supplies user.email, Git continues resolving the include against the isolated HOME and silently loses the identity. This is especially clear for a user who has only the XDG global config: includeRealGitConfig returns here before creating a rewriter at all. Apply the preservation logic to both native global sources, maintaining their order, and cover a ~/ include originating in the XDG file with XDG both set and unset. The new effective-Git test starts the chain only from ~/.gitconfig and misses this remaining instance of the previous finding.

[P2] Parse continued include values before rewriting physical lines

Git permits a config assignment to continue onto the next physical line using a trailing backslash, but rewrite, hasHomeRelativeInclude and gitIncludeTargets each process one physical line at a time. A valid two-line assignment consisting of `path = ~/` followed by a trailing backslash, then `.gitconfig-work` on the next line, originally includes ~/.gitconfig-work. This code detects the ~/ prefix, rewrites only the first line as a complete quoted assignment, and leaves the .gitconfig-work line behind as an invalid variable name. The generated global config then makes Git commands fail while parsing configuration. Handle logical lines and Git escaping consistently before discovering or rewriting includes, and add an effective-Git regression for a continued include value. Git's continuation rule is documented at https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#_syntax.

Fixed in `2b48b65f0c`.

`gitConfigRewriter.rewrite` now treats `[includeIf "..."]` as a path directive when the condition starts with `gitdir:` or `gitdir/i:`, and anchors the pattern the way it already anchored include paths:

- `gitdir:./...` is resolved against the directory of the config being copied (the real one) and `gitdir:~/...` against the real home, so the relocated copy keeps the original base instead of pointing at `.ao-gitconfig`.
- Globs survive (`~/projects/**` becomes `<real-home>/projects/**`), `gitdir/i` keeps its case-insensitive keyword, and a trailing `/` is preserved because git matches that separator literally (it appends `**` to it).
- Absolute patterns, `~user`, bare globs (matched anywhere), and `onbranch:` are left untouched.
- A `~/` condition now triggers materialization on its own. Previously only a `~/` include path did, so a config whose single home-dependent element was a condition would have been included in place and still seen the redirected HOME.

`TestPrepareSessionHomeAnchorsConditionalIncludeHeaders` initialises two real repositories under the real home and runs `git config --list` inside each with the session home as `HOME`: the `gitdir:./` include must still supply `user.email`, `gitdir/i:~/projects/**` must match the projects repository and only that one, and the session-owned copy must carry the anchored base. You were right that the old `/nonexistent/` case could not catch this; the new test fails without the rewrite because the condition then resolves under `.ao-gitconfig`.

Fixed in `2b48b65f0c`.

`mirrorUserGitConfig` and `includeRealGitConfig` are now one `preserveGitConfiguration` that feeds both native global sources, in the order git reads them:

- **XDG set** (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` absolute): the real file stays on native discovery. If its chain depends on a HOME-relative base, the anchored copy is materialised and included from the session `~/.gitconfig` *ahead of* the real `~/.gitconfig`, so re-applying it cannot invert precedence. A user whose only global file is the XDG one now gets it too, because the block is written even when `~/.gitconfig` does not exist.
- **XDG unset**: `$HOME/.config/git/config` resolves inside the session home, so the mirrored file is the file git actually reads. It is rewritten in place, with its includes and conditions resolved against the real XDG directory, because the mirror's own location is no longer the original base.

`TestPrepareSessionHomeAnchorsXDGGlobalIncludes` runs both layouts through real git, with a `~/` include, a relative include, and `core.pager` set in both files: the XDG values resolve (`user.email`, `commit.template`, `core.excludesfile`), and `~/.gitconfig` still wins on `core.pager`, which pins the native order rather than only checking presence.

Fixed in `2b48b65f0c`.

Config parsing now works on git's logical lines. `splitGitConfigLines` joins a physical line ending in an unescaped backslash with the next one (an odd trailing-backslash count continues, an even one does not), strips the CR that git ignores in CRLF files, and keeps the original bytes alongside the joined text. Detection (`needsGitConfigAnchoring`, `gitIncludeTargets`), condition parsing, and rewriting all read the joined text, and a rewritten include is emitted as one complete quoted assignment, so the continuation disappears with the line it belonged to. Lines that are not rewritten keep their raw bytes, continuations included, so nothing else is reformatted.

`TestPrepareSessionHomeJoinsContinuedIncludeValues` uses the exact shape from the review (`path = ~/` followed by a trailing backslash, then `.gitconfig-work`) and asserts through real git that the include resolves and the config parses at all; a CRLF subtest covers the same path with `\r\n` endings. It also checks that an untouched continued `alias` value keeps its original spelling in the session-owned copy, so collapsing continuations stays local to the lines being rewritten.

One related hardening while I was in there: a copy is registered before its contents are written, so a cyclic include chain resolves to a path instead of recursing.

[P2] Avoid reading the XDG config twice when applying its rewritten copy

With an absolute XDG_CONFIG_HOME, Git still loads the real XDG git/config through native discovery. This branch then includes a materialized copy of that entire file from the session .gitconfig whenever any include or condition needs anchoring. Direct settings and already-working include chains are therefore read twice. That preserves last-value-wins settings, but changes multivalued configuration: for example, an XDG file with http.extraHeader = Authorization: Bearer <token> plus an include path = ~/.gitconfig-work now produces two Authorization headers instead of one, potentially breaking HTTPS authentication. Git explicitly adds every http.extraHeader entry: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#Documentation/git-config.txt-httpextraHeader.

Arrange for the anchored XDG configuration to be read exactly once, while keeping XDG-before-.gitconfig precedence and leaving the real file untouched. Add an effective-Git regression using git config --get-all http.extraHeader (and an existing absolute XDG_CONFIG_HOME). The current effectiveGitConfig helper stores values in a map, so duplicate entries are discarded and the added test cannot detect this regression.

[P1] Handle pointer capture before releasing cancelled mouse input

Moving to (-1,-1) prevents an ordinary button from receiving the release, but active pointer capture routes the release back to the capturing element regardless of its coordinates.

Reproduced with the current TrustedInput implementation unchanged against real Chrome 155.0.8059.85, using a form's Submit button with this handler:

```js
button.addEventListener('pointerdown', event => button.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId));
```

Abort immediately after the actual CDP mousePressed resolves: cleanup still produces mouseup, click, and form submit after cancellation, while the command returns BROWSER_COMMAND_CANCELED. The same reproduction confirms that normal clicks submit and cancelled ordinary buttons no longer activate, so this is specifically the pointer-capture case missing from the new regression.

Handle active pointer capture before the cleanup release and add this case to the real-browser regression test so cancellation cannot complete the button activation.

[P2] Do not reclaim a lock from a stale ownership observation

The timestamp check and this removal are separate operations. A can read an expired lock and pause, then B removes it, acquires a fresh lock, and starts repairing the corrupt key. When A resumes, it removes B's live lock, acquires its own, repairs the key, and returns token A. B then resumes its previously guarded rename, displaces A's valid key, and returns token B. A deterministic two-process reproduction against the actual module and real filesystem confirmed that A deleted the new owner's lock, the tokens diverged, and the first returned token no longer matched disk. Make stale-lock reclamation and release ownership-safe, and cover the stale-check-to-remove interleaving.

**P1: spawn trusts a saved catalog AO has already marked out of date, and never checks effort.**

`savedCatalogCovers` only checks `Stale`, an empty list, and that the model ID is present. Two cases slip through:

1. **`RefreshState` is ignored.** `InvalidateModelCatalogs` (after an install/update or auth change) requeues saved rows as `queued`. For claude-code the read path also reports `refreshing` while the background inputs check runs. Spawn validates against that row anyway. Example: switching Claude Code from the Anthropic API to Bedrock (model IDs differ by provider). A spawn with the old Anthropic ID still matches the saved list. Previously that failed cleanly with `ErrUnsupportedModel` ("not in the active provider catalog"); now it passes validation and fails later in the CLI.
2. **Effort isn't part of coverage.** If the model is listed but the requested effort isn't, there's no rediscovery, so `ErrUnsupportedEffort` comes back. Example: after a Claude Code update adds an effort level, a spawn asking for it (API, `ao spawn`, project default effort) fails until the background revalidation lands. It used to succeed because spawn always ran `refresh=true`. Codex hides this through the leave-it-to-the-CLI fallback; Claude Code doesn't.

Suggestion: treat the saved catalog as covering only when `RefreshState` is `""`/`idle` (not `queued`/`refreshing`/`error`) and, when an effort is requested, the selected model lists it. Alternatively, retry once with `refresh=true` whenever validation would otherwise fail. A test each for "queued catalog" and "effort missing from saved list" would pin it down; `provision_test.go` currently covers only the missing-model case.

**P2: a spawn's rediscovery can now wait an extra 30 s at startup.**

This wait applies to every load, including `modelLoadRefresh`. Spawn's `refresh=true` call also joins any in-flight load for the same key (for example the background first-load started by the `Models(..., false)` call just before it). So a spawn shortly after daemon start, for an agent without a usable saved catalog, can take up to ~30 s readiness + ~30 s discovery instead of ~30 s. Startup restores and orchestrator spawns are the likely victims. Consider skipping the readiness wait for `modelLoadRefresh`, or at least for spawn-driven loads.

**P3: a stale "not installed" result blocks discovery, including an explicit refresh.**

`Snapshot()` returns the last observation and doesn't re-probe. It marks expired entries `Freshness: stale`, but this check ignores freshness. When `model`/`mode`/`effort` are sent, `harness` should be sent too. Otherwise the model is stored against a harness the automation doesn't pin.

`ao automation create` without `--harness` stores `harness: ""` ("empty uses project default"). If you edit that automation here, `harness` state stays `""`, so `harnessChanged` is false and only `model` (and maybe `effort`) is saved. The picker listed models for `selectedHarness = projectDefaultWorker || fallbackHarness`, but at run time the scheduler spawns with `Harness: ""`, which the daemon resolves on its own. If the project's default worker later changes from Codex to Claude Code, the stored `gpt-5` is validated against Claude's catalog, and every scheduled run fails. If the project has no default worker at all, the menu showed `fallbackHarness` models that may not match what the daemon picks.

The create form has a related race. `useProjectDefaultWorker` resolves asynchronously, so a model picked while `selectedHarness` was still `fallbackHarness` survives the switch to the project default. The `AgentModelField` key changes, but the model/effort state isn't cleared.

Possible fix: include `harness: selectedHarness` whenever a model/mode/effort is persisted, and clear model/mode/effort when `selectedHarness` changes, not only when the user changes the harness.

The form clears model/mode/effort when the harness changes, but nothing here does. `ao automation update <id> --harness amp` (or a PATCH with only `harness`) keeps the stored `model: gpt-5, effort: high`.

The scheduler then sends `EffortOverride: true` with `Effort: "high"` for Amp. `resolveAgentConfig` rejects that with `ErrUnsupportedEffort`, so every occurrence fails. Switching to `claude-code` gets a similar failure from Claude's model validation.

Suggest clearing `Model`/`Mode`/`Effort` here when the harness actually changes and the request doesn't set them, which matches the UI. A service test for that case would lock it in.

When an automation has no saved model, it falls back to the catalog's `isDefault` model. But a spawn with an empty model inherits the project's worker config (`effectiveAgentConfig` → `projectConfig.worker.agentConfig.model`/`effort`), not the catalog default.

Example: the project worker is set to `capable` / `low`. Every existing automation then shows "GPT-5 · High" in this picker while it actually runs `capable` / `low`.

It also affects what gets saved. If the user changes only Effort, the form saves `model: ""` plus an effort chosen from GPT-5's levels. That effort is applied to the project model at spawn time, which may not support it.

New Task avoids this by seeding from `projectModelForSelectedAgent`/`defaultWorkerEffort` when the selected agent is the project's agent. The automation form probably needs the same seeding, or an explicit "Project default" label for the empty value.

`probeCtx` (20s, `authProbeTimeout`) is derived from the coordinator's ctx, which is also 20s for MiMo (`readiness_coordinator.go:617`), so they share one deadline. That deadline has to cover `auth list` plus `debug config`, `debug paths`, `models` (each a separate `mimo` process) plus the 8s HTTP probe. If it runs out, `ctx.Err()` is `DeadlineExceeded` and the coordinator records `AuthCheckTimeout` as a failure and schedules retries, where before this PR a detected credential returned `configured, nil`.

Suggestion: give verification its own budget, and treat a verification timeout as inconclusive by returning `AgentAuthStatusConfigured, nil` with a `probe_timeout` diagnostic. Only propagate `ctx.Err()` when the credential-detection step itself didn't finish.

Same pattern as MiMo: if `hermes status` (up to 30s) plus binary resolution plus the 8s probe pushes past the 45s coordinator budget, returning `ctx.Err()` turns an already-established `configured` result into an auth-check timeout failure. The provider-unsupported branch at L129 also now returns `ctx.Err()` where it previously returned `nil`. I'd return `nil` here and let `VerifyConnection`'s `probe_timeout`/`probe_cancelled` diagnostic carry the inconclusive result.

This relabels every `configured` harness as "Credentials not verified", not just MiMo/Hermes after a failed or inconclusive probe. Cases that look wrong:

- **MiMo Auto free channel**: `mimocode/auth.go` returns `configured` when only `mimo/mimo-auto` is listed and no credentials exist.
- **Claude Code `token_renewal_pending`**: the coordinator's reason says "is signed in; its access token renews the next time it runs, so no action is needed".
- **Harnesses that never verify** (Claude Code when its validation rung can't answer, codewhale, memcode, unrealagent): there's nothing the user can do to clear the warning.

Could this be keyed on the diagnostics (for example, only when a `provider_validation` step ran and came back inconclusive or unsupported), with a neutral label otherwise?

This interacts with the new backend reset in `Update`. Pinning an unpinned automation sends only the fields that changed, but the backend now clears every *omitted* field when the harness goes from `""` to `codex`.

The `pins the harness for an effort-only edit` test shows it. The saved state is `{harness: "", model: "capable"}`, the user changes only Effort, and the form sends `{harness: "codex", effort: "low"}`. The test explicitly asserts that `model` is absent. On the server, `rec.Harness != *input.Harness` wipes `Model`, and nothing restores it. The automation then runs on the project/catalog default with an effort chosen for `capable`.

Related: when editing such an automation before the `["project", id]` query is cached, the effect at L334 records `selectedHarness` as the fallback harness. Then it sees the project default resolve and clears the hydrated model/effort. Any later save, even a rename, sends `model: ""`/`effort: ""`.

Suggested fix: when `harnessChanged` is true, send all three tuning fields explicitly (`{ model, mode, effort, harness: selectedHarness }`), so the request doesn't depend on the server's omitted-field rule. For the hydration case, seed `previousHarness` only after the project defaults have loaded when `automation.harness` is empty.

`UpdateArtifactShare` changes `name` (taken from the PUT query) but leaves `document_key` (`baseSlug/oldName`) as it was. Once a link is renamed by PUT, its document identity no longer matches what it serves:

- `POST ?project=p&feature=f&name=new.html` is treated as a new document and takes another slot (or hits the limit), even though a link for `new.html` already exists.
- `POST ... name=old.html` replaces the link that now serves `new.html`.

Please either reject a PUT whose `name` differs from the stored name (it is part of the document key), or update `document_key` in the same statement and map the unique-index conflict on `(user_id, document_key)` to a 409. Please also add a handler test for the case you choose.

Fixed in 64d240959f by rejecting the rename. The handler compares the PUT's `name` with the link's stored name before uploading anything, and returns `409 artifact_share_name_changed` ("A share link keeps its file name. Publish the renamed file as a new link."). `UpdateArtifactShare` also checks the name under the row lock, returns `ErrArtifactShareNameChanged`, and no longer writes `name`, so the name and `document_key` can't drift even if another caller skips the handler.

`TestArtifactSharePutRejectsAnotherFileName` covers both of your cases: a refused rename stores nothing, and the link keeps serving `old.html`. After that, `POST name=new.html` creates a new link, and `POST name=old.html` replaces the original link (`replaced: true`, still named `old.html`), leaving the `new.html` link alone. A PUT with the same name still works. The Postgres store test checks the store-level refusal, and the contract documents the 409.

**Bug: the anonymous ID changes on every restart while a Cloud user is bound.** `NewIdentity` doesn't restore `cloudUserID`, which stays empty until the desktop calls `POST /internal/telemetry/identity` again. So every event from daemon start until that call (`ao.daemon.started`, etc.) goes out under this new `anon_<uuid>`, and that ID is never saved.

Before this PR those events used the install ID, which `identify()` had already merged into the user, so they joined the person. Now each restart creates a new distinct_id. For a headless or CLI-only daemon with no renderer to re-bind, that happens on every start indefinitely, which inflates unique-user counts.

The tests miss it because they always call `SetCloudUserID` straight after construction. Suggested fix: write this ID to `telemetry_anonymous_id` when it's generated, so it stays the same across restarts. Also add a test that constructs an identity from a dir with `telemetry_bound_user` set, then constructs it again, and checks that `Snapshot().DistinctID()` matches.

**Create-then-write isn't atomic, and an empty file is now fatal.** `O_EXCL` creates an empty file and the ID is written afterwards. If the process crashes between the two steps, or Electron main reads the file in that window on first launch (the TS side has the same `wx` open-then-write), the file is empty. Lines 727 and 739 now treat an empty file as a hard error, where it used to be regenerated.

Result: `NewPostHogSink` and `standaloneIdentity` fail on every start from then on. PostHog is disabled, the phone identity route has no store, and through the `daemon.go` change daemon Sentry is turned off too. The renderer's `buildTelemetryBootstrap` also throws. Nothing recovers from it automatically.

Suggested fix: write to a temp file and then `os.Link` it into place (fails if the target exists) or rename it, so the file is never visible empty. Keep treating an empty or whitespace-only file as "regenerate" so a corrupt file heals itself. Apply the same fix in `frontend/src/shared/telemetry.ts:69`, where the `EEXIST` retry can read the half-written file and throw.

Same issue as `posthog.go:732`. If the daemon has just `O_EXCL`-created the file but hasn't written it yet, this throws, and the `EEXIST` retry path on the write side can hit it too. An empty file used to mean regenerate; now `buildTelemetryBootstrap` rejects. Consider treating empty as missing, together with an atomic create on both sides.

**Unrequested behaviour change: Sentry now depends on the telemetry identity.** `installID` is empty whenever `cfg.DataDir == ""` or `NewIdentity` fails, for example on an unreadable or empty `telemetry_install_id` (see the `posthog.go` comment). In those cases daemon crash and 5xx reporting is silently turned off, even with a valid DSN and consent.

A missing tag shouldn't disable error reporting. Suggest keeping the DSN and simply leaving out the `install_id` tag when it isn't available; `applyTags` already handles an empty ID. If the gating is intentional, please give the reason in the PR description and `docs/telemetry.md`.

**Small bug: `adoptedKey` isn't cleared here.** When the desktop is opted in but reports no `distinctId`, this branch nulls `pairedInstallId`, `cloudUserId` and `githubActor` but leaves `adoptedKey` set. If the next refresh returns the same identity as before, `key === adoptedKey` returns early before those fields are filled in again. Every event then carries `ao_cloud_user_id: null` and no `paired_install_id` until the key changes. Set `adoptedKey = null` here, as the `!identity` branch does.

The clear-and-unregister block is also identical to the one at lines 154-163. Pulling it into a `clearPairedAttribution()` helper would fix this and remove the duplicate.

nit: this fingerprint includes `cfg.password`, so the bearer password is kept in a long-lived closure string only to detect config changes. `hostId` + `host` + `httpPort` + `secure` should be enough to detect a host switch. If a re-pair with a new password also needs to reset attribution, consider comparing a hash or a pairing generation counter instead.

On Windows with a Chromium browser (Brave here), "works on background windows" didn't hold in practice. Chromium throttles or stops painting occluded and background windows. `get_window_state` returned a blank page more than once, and a lazily loaded dialog (a post composer) never got past its loading skeleton, even after reloads. A foreground F5 sometimes got the page back, but never the dialog.

The agent has no tool to bring a window to the front, so it kept retrying. Could the guide name this limitation, for Windows and Chromium-based browsers at least? Something like: "if a window reads blank or stuck loading twice, ask the user to bring it to the front rather than retrying." And if the driver has an activate or raise step, it could be exposed as a `run_steps` step.

The read after an action comes back `ok: true` even when the window hasn't painted: a near-empty tree and a blank screenshot. In the Windows test the agent only worked this out from the screenshot after several actions.

A cheap guard might help. When the read has very few `elements` (or the tree only has the frame), add a hint to `observation`: "the window may not be rendered, possibly because it's in the background; ask the user to bring it to the front." That would cut the reload loop short. Each extra iteration costs a screenshot, roughly 1 to 1.5k tokens.

Seen once on Windows and Brave: a click by element token on a page that was still loading landed on a neighbouring element (it hovered a card instead of opening the "start a post" button). The agent fell back to a pixel click with `pid`/`window_id`, which the window check allowed, as intended. The pixel click opened the composer.

This is likely the same background-render problem: the tree's layout and what Chromium had actually laid out had drifted apart. It might be worth a line here: "if a click by token didn't do what the screenshot expected, read again before falling back to pixels."

This worked well in the Windows test. The agent spotted that the browser was signed in to someone other than the person asking. It said so before trying the composer, and offered to stop or wait for the right account.

One idea: name that check explicitly here or in `cua.md`'s Safety section, for example "before anything outward-facing, confirm which account the app is signed in to." A shared machine or browser profile makes that the easiest way to post as the wrong person.

When the user explicitly asks to use *their* browser (their signed-in profile), the agent reasonably drove it with computer use, not `ao browser`. Given the background-paint problem on Windows, it might help to tell the agent when to pick which. For example: "prefer `ao browser`; drive a native browser only when the user asks for it or needs its signed-in session, and expect it to have to stay in the foreground on Windows."

Thanks, that matches the background-throttling behaviour of Chromium-based apps. Fixed in 4a71e3dd0:

- The workflow no longer promises that acting by element always works on background windows. It now says "usually", and points to a new note.
- The new note says that Chromium-based browsers and apps (Chrome, Brave, Edge, Electron), on Windows especially, can stop painting windows that are hidden behind others. `get_window_state` can then read a blank page, or a lazily loaded dialog stuck on its loading skeleton. After two blank or stuck reads, the agent should stop retrying and ask the user to bring the window to the front and leave it visible, then read again.

About a raise step: Cua Driver has `bring_to_front`, but it can't be a `run_steps` step, because steps are limited to input actions (click, type, keys, scroll, drag, set_value). It also leaves the app in the foreground for good, which takes focus away from someone using the machine, so I haven't added it as an agent tool. The per-action `delivery_mode: "foreground"` only fronts the window for that one action and then restores the user's app, so it doesn't keep a page painting. The guide now says both, so the agent asks the user instead of looping.

Good idea, done in d94e3c0f2 (plus 8fa8b73c1, a lint fix).

Every window read the agent sees now gets a `render_warning` when it looks unpainted. That covers a direct `get_window_state`, the read AO does after each action, and `run_steps`' observation. A read counts as unpainted when either:
- the tree is only the frame (fewer than 3 elements), or
- the screenshot is blank: 98% of a 48x48 pixel sample is one colour.

The agent's text shows it as a `warning:` line under the window line. It says not to retry, and to ask the user to bring the window to the front and leave it visible.

The screenshot check is there because a background Chromium window usually still has its tabs and address bar in the tree, so counting elements alone wouldn't catch a blank page. One case it doesn't catch is a dialog stuck on a loading skeleton, since that's neither empty nor one colour. The guide's "two blank or stuck reads, then ask the user" rule from the previous thread covers that.

Tested with unit tests: frame-only tree, blank screenshot, painted window, tree-only and screenshot-only reads, the warning reaching the result after an action, and the text output. Also checked live with Cua Driver 0.37.0: a macOS window on another Space read as 0 elements and got the warning. I couldn't test Windows here.

**[spec] Foreground delivery gets past the "don't act where the user is working" checks.** I verified this on Windows. `press_key` with `{"pid":…, "window_id":…, "delivery_mode":"foreground"}` was accepted, and the driver reported `route: global_input` and `Sent end via SendInput`. That raises the window and sends real input to whatever has focus. It's exactly the case the desktop-scope and window checks exist to prevent.

`run_steps` also accepts `foreground_fallback` and `delivery_mode`. And the driver's own background result *suggests* it: `If it didn't land, retry with delivery_mode:"foreground"`.

Options:
- refuse `delivery_mode:"foreground"` and `foreground_fallback:true` here, with an AO hint (like the `desktop_scope_disabled` rewrite);
- or add them to `hiddenArguments`;
- or allow them deliberately, and make the guide's safety section say to confirm with the user first.

The last option is also the only fix for the background-paint problem from my earlier review, so this needs an explicit decision.

**[spec] The toggle itself is reachable from the LAN.** `/api/v1/computer-use` is blocked here, but `PATCH /api/v1/settings/computer-use` is not. `isLANControlBlockedRequest` only covers agent installs.

The renderer-origin guard in `cors.go` doesn't stop a paired phone. So a paired device can turn on "Let agents use this computer", and every new chat on the desktop then gets desktop control. Suggest adding `/api/v1/settings/computer-use` to the blocked prefixes. Its segment-boundary match won't catch the other settings routes.

**[spec] `Call` doesn't check the toggle, and runs any driver tool except the browser ones.** The description says computer use is gated by "Let agents use this computer", and that terminal sessions get none. But `POST /computer-use/call` works with the toggle off. It also passes through tools outside the 7 offered (the driver has others, such as desktop-wide state and script runners), limited only by `toolNamePattern` and the browser blocklist.

The route is loopback-only and origin-guarded. Any local process can still use it, though, including an agent in a terminal session that has `curl`.

Suggest two checks here:
- refuse with `COMPUTER_USE_DISABLED` while the setting is off;
- allow only the offered tools plus the step-only ones `run_steps` needs, or otherwise refuse what isn't offered.

**[spec]** The description says "The switch needs Cua Driver installed before it can be turned on." Only the renderer enforces this (`ComputerUseSection.tsx:272`). `SetComputerUse(ctx, true)` succeeds with no driver, so the API or an older client can turn it on.

It isn't harmful, because the tools then fail with `COMPUTER_USE_NOT_INSTALLED`. But the rule should live server-side if it's part of the contract. Otherwise, drop it from the description.

**[spec]** The description says "When an idle driver session has ended, AO revives it with `start_session` and retries once." That revival lives in `Call`. This read after an action goes straight to `callWithDaemon`.

If the driver session expires between the action and the read, the agent gets `observation.ok:false` with a session-ended error even though the action landed. Rare, but it's the read the guide tells the agent to trust. Consider routing the read through the same revive-and-retry path.

**[standards] Status code.** Every driver refusal maps to `KindUnavailable` (HTTP 503), including `invalid_arguments` (seen on Windows: `run_steps: unknown argument scope` came back 503) and `Missing required integer field: pid`. 503 tells HTTP clients and retries that the service is down.

Suggest mapping driver `refused` / `invalid_arguments` to `KindInvalid` (400), and keeping 503 for a missing or unreachable driver.

**[P2, non-blocking while development-only] Lock the predecessor before replacing a document's share.**

This SELECT reads version A without a row lock. A concurrent PUT can install B and queue A; POST then installs C but queues its stale snapshot A. B is no longer served and was already removed from the upload queue by PUT, so it is never collected. The per-user advisory lock serializes POSTs only; PUT does not acquire it.

Reproduced on scratch PostgreSQL using the production store methods: pause POST after this read, complete PUT, resume POST, and the collection queue contains A but omits B. [P1] Use one-shot approvals for client-side bypass

Choosing allow_always before allow_once gives bypass a lifetime beyond the selected AO mode. In Hermes v0.22.2, acp_adapter/permissions.py offers allow_session with kind allow_always before its permanent allow_always option, and maps that choice to session. tools/approval.py then persists the command pattern in _session_approved and checks that cache before requesting permission again. Hermes' set_session_mode(default) only changes its edit-approval mode; it does not clear this command cache. Thus a dangerous command approved during bypass can execute again without prompting after the user changes to Default, even with the new explicit mode mapping. Prefer allow_once for automatic bypass responses so each subsequent request is governed by the current AO policy, and add a regression covering bypass -> approved command -> Default -> the same command pattern.

Upstream evidence: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/v0.22.2/acp_adapter/permissions.py (_build_permission_options and _OPTION_ID_TO_HERMES), https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/v0.22.2/tools/approval.py (_persist_choice and is_approved), and https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/v0.22.2/acp_adapter/server.py (set_session_mode).

[P2] Retain permission identity when the request precedes its notification

When permission-request arrives while Active, this branch records only the sequence number. The subsequent notification sets copilotPermissionWaiting but resets the tool name/candidate to empty, so even a matching pre-tool-use cannot clear waiting_input; post-tool-use is sticky-suppressed too. AO can stay Input needed throughout an approved tool execution until stop. This ordering is expected: Copilot's [hook contract](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference#permissionrequest-decision-control) places permissionRequest before user prompting, while notification is asynchronous. The tests put notification first; the second-approval test uses request first but ends before testing its resolution. Preserve request identity across notification entry and cover request -> notification -> approved tool -> completion.

[P2] Handle completed permission cycles without a tool-use ID

The new stale-notification guard only consumes a cycle when copilotAwaitPostToolUseID is nonempty. Copilot's documented camelCase pre/post payloads contain toolName but no toolUseId, and the CLI tests here use that ID-less shape. In the covered notification -> permission-request -> matching pre -> post flow with those real payloads, copilotAwaitPostToolUseID stays empty and copilotConsumedPermReqSeq stays zero. A delayed notification then re-enters waiting_input even though the tool finished. The lifecycle stale-notification tests hide this by supplying synthetic toolu_* IDs. Please cover the documented ID-less payloads and reconcile completion without requiring an unavailable ID. [Payload reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference#hook-event-input-payloads).

[P2] Reopen notification handling after an elicitation answer

The existing elicitation flow clears waiting_input via user-prompt-submit, but this branch simultaneously sets copilotSuppressNotifyAfterStop. That flag is checked before permission-cycle counters and is never cleared by a fresh permission-request. Thus notification(elicitation) -> user-prompt-submit(answer) -> permission-request(next tool) -> notification(permission_prompt) leaves AO Active while Copilot is awaiting approval. All later notifications remain suppressed until another user-prompt-submit arrives from a non-input state. Blocker: the standard npm Windows shim (cmd-shim) always fails here. Its `@CALL :find_dp0` line matches `call\s+` with an extensionless target, so `requireInspection` is true, `discoveryLauncherTarget` returns `""`, and discovery fails with `cannot verify launcher command ":find_dp0"`.

That breaks every npm-installed agent on Windows (grok-cli, pi, kilocode, copilot, auggie, opencode-ai, ...). The "npm shim" test uses a simplified one-line shim, so it doesn't catch this. Please test against the real cmd-shim output.

Blocker: POSIX launchers that `exec` a variable or use `exec -a` get rejected:
- Cursor's `~/.local/share/cursor-agent/versions/<v>/cursor-agent` runs `exec -a "$0" "$NODE_BIN" ...`, so the invoked target is taken as `-a`, giving `cannot verify launcher command "-a"`.
- pnpm shims run `exec "$basedir/node" ...` and `exec node ...`.
- `exec "$@"` and `. "$HOME/.profile"` fail the same way.

Separately, only the first word of a line is treated as the command being run. So `@npx autohand %*`, `start "" /b autohand %*`, `env autohand`, `if exist ... ( autohand )` and `a && autohand` are never checked, and the agent-named wrapper alone still makes `verified=true`. That is the Autohand overwrite this PR is meant to stop.

Blocker: native binaries whose resolved name isn't an agent name return `verified=false`, so version-manager shims are refused outright. For example, `~/.local/share/mise/shims/grok` links to `mise`, and `~/.volta/bin/<agent>` links to `volta-shim`. After `EvalSymlinks` the owner is `""`, this returns false, and the user gets `cannot verify executable ... belongs to grok` every time. The same applies to any renamed or versioned native target that doesn't match `discoveryVersionedExecutable`.

Any extensionless `cmd` at the start of a line maps to command-code, so an ordinary `cmd /c "%~dp0grok.exe" %*` in a `.cmd`/`.ps1` launcher is rejected with the misleading `launcher redirects to command-code instead of grok`.

A UTF-8 BOM isn't stripped. Only UTF-16 is decoded above, and `TrimSpace` doesn't remove U+FEFF. So for a BOM-prefixed `grok.ps1` containing `\ufeff& autohand @args`, the `&` prefix group doesn't match, the target becomes the BOM character, `autohand` is never checked, and the file name makes it verified. Strip `\xEF\xBB\xBF` before splitting lines.

`verified` is an OR over every reference on every line, including ones that are never executed (`IF EXIST`, `SET`, `echo`). Only agents in `discoveryExecutableOwners` count as foreign. So `IF EXIST "%~dp0grok.exe" echo ok` followed by `"%~dp0gemini.exe" %*` passes: `grok.exe` vouches for the file, and gemini/qwen/goose have no owner entry, so they are allowed.

The check covers only command-backed and FX model discovery. Cursor `AuthStatus` (`cursor-agent status` via authprobe), codex app-server discovery, ACP option discovery and the Claude probes still run the same unchecked binary. If Cursor's `agent.cmd` has been overwritten to launch Autohand, model discovery is now refused, but the auth probe can still start Autohand's device login and open a browser. Putting this in binary resolution (`ResolveBinary`) or the shared probe/`modelCommand` path would cover all of these.

Returning the symlink-resolved path changes what discovery runs, compared with the PATH entry. A multi-call CLI that picks its mode from `argv[0]` now gets the canonical name, which matters for aliases like `ah` or `opencode2`. For npm/bun bin symlinks it now executes `node_modules/.../cli.js` directly, which fails with permission denied or an exec format error if that file has no exec bit or shebang. Suggest verifying against the resolved path but still running the original `LookPath` result.

Nit: `EvalSymlinks` already ran at line 35 for the root, and a line-start quoted target that also matches `discoveryLauncherReference` is added to `references` twice, so it is read twice. For example, `"%~dp0grok.exe" %*`. The recursion is also limited only by depth 8, with no overall budget. Dedupe references per line and keep a visited/total-files limit.

Blocker: the effort is restored unconditionally, but the model only `if rec.Metadata.Model != ""`. Because the config is sent with `AgentConfigResolved: true`, nothing checks the resulting pair against the catalog, and the `modelChangedWithoutExplicitEffort` clearing doesn't run either. Ways to hit this:

1. **Empty saved model:** a Codex task created on the provider-default model at `xhigh` fails to start. The project default model then changes to one that only supports low/medium. Retry launches the new model with `xhigh`, which is rejected, and every Retry after that fails too.
2. **Model changed in ChatUI before Retry:** `PersistChatModel` (manager.go:3763) updates only the model, so the newly picked model is paired with the effort saved at creation.
3. **Catalog drift:** if the provider stops offering `xhigh` for the saved model between the failure and the Retry, the old effort goes out without validation. The retry fails at the provider instead of returning `ErrUnsupportedEffort` early or falling back.

Please check the effort against the model actually being launched, and clear it or fall back when they don't match.

Two related points:
- **Two meanings of an empty effort.** Here an empty `Metadata.Effort` means "provider default", but `resumeAgentRecordWithPolicy` (manager.go:3465, `if effort != ""`) treats the same empty value as "inherit the project default". The same session gets a different effort depending on which restore path runs.
- **The fix belongs in `restoredAgentConfig`.** It already restores model and effort for Claude Code (manager.go:2264-2267), so this line does nothing for Claude and duplicates the logic for everyone else. Moving the harness-independent model/effort/permissions restore into one helper used by both retry and resume would fix this in one place, so the next restore caller can't miss it.

The "unspecified" cases only start with an empty project default. When there is a default (say `medium`) and the user picks no effort, `Spawn` saves the resolved default into `Metadata.Effort` (manager.go:1059-1062). So it is pinned, not left unspecified as the PR description says. If the default then changes to `low`, Retry runs at `medium`. Please add a case for this, and adjust the description or behavior to match the intent.

All cases use Codex with an explicit `gpt-test` model. Please add cases for (a) `Model: ""`, saved effort `xhigh`, and a project default model changed before Retry to one without `xhigh`, and (b) the model changed via `PersistChatModel` before Retry. Those are the combinations where the conditional model restore and the unconditional effort restore conflict, and the current suite passes without covering them.

`scrollToFn`, which handles the virtualizer's end-anchoring and `resizeItem` adjustments, still writes `scrollTop` during a reader hold, and its `markWritten` wipes `readerIntentFrom`. The new hold guard covers `followOrSnapToEnd` only.

Scenario: virtualized and pinned at the end while streaming, the reader presses PageUp or wheels up. `hold()` records the intent and Chromium starts the smooth scroll. In the same frame, the streaming row's ResizeObserver fires `resizeItem`. `wasAtEnd` is true, so `applyScrollAdjustment` calls `scrollToFn`, which sets `scrollTop += growth`. That aborts the browser animation and nulls the intent, and the scroll event then lands on `lastWritten`, so the keypress is eaten. `scrollToFn` should return early (or defer) while `isHeld()`.

Related: `scrollEndThreshold` reads the React `pinned` state, not `pinnedRef`. Between `releaseFollow` and the next render, the virtualizer still end-anchors, and since `getVirtualDistanceFromEnd()` excludes the prompt spacer, a reader inside the spacer band still counts as at the end and gets pushed down.

Regression: the wheel hold seeds `readerIntentFrom` from `lastScrollTop`, which is stale until the next scroll event, rather than `node.scrollTop`. Scenario: pinned at 5000, content shrinks, and the browser clamps or `scrollToFn` writes 4900, clearing the intent. Before that scroll event dispatches, the reader wheels up over a code block that consumes the wheel. `hold(250, 5000)` then makes our own pending event at 4900 match `top < readerIntentFrom - 2`, so it's classified as the reader and calls `releaseFollow`. Auto-follow stops and "Jump to latest" appears although the log never moved. Keyboard and touch holds already use `node.scrollTop`.

The new `isHeld()` early return drops the initial snap instead of deferring it, and nothing catches up when the hold expires. If the last measurement lands inside a 250ms hold during the first second and no more resizes follow, the chat opens mid-history while still `pinned`. Note that `onTouchMove` holds on any direction. With `pinned=true`, the Jump-to-latest button is hidden too.

`markWritten` nulls `readerIntentFrom` instead of re-basing it to the written top, so any app-owned write during a hold disables the reader-intent classifier for the rest of the gesture. Small trackpad steps (1–2px) right after a virtualizer write fall within `OWN_SCROLL_PX` of `lastWritten` and are treated as ours. Re-basing (`readerIntentFrom = top` while held) keeps the guard working.

**The parser misses some ways of running a command (low).** None of these break existing installs, but they let a redirect through:

- Commands behind `command`, `nohup`, `time`, `sh -c` or `bash -c` are never seen. For example, `command autohand "$@"` only reports `command` as the target.

[P2] Reserve a unique screenshot filename across calls

`savedImages` is new for each request, so both `count` and the millisecond timestamp can coincide for concurrent same-tool calls in the same session (including the shared empty-session scope). Those requests then write/adopt the same file, allowing one window's image to replace another window's image while its tree/token header stays unchanged. A bounded probe through the real service/externalization code, with 64 concurrent fake-driver reads and distinct synthetic PNGs, overwrote 61–62 of the 64 outputs in three independent reruns. Different sessions did not collide. Reserve a unique per-call suffix or exclusive file rather than using only a per-call counter and millisecond time. This is an isolated backend reproduction, not a native-driver concurrency measurement.

[P2] Strip caller screenshot paths when batch observation opts out

With a caller-supplied `observe:{include_screenshot:false,screenshot_out_file:"/absolute/outside-ao.png"}`, this branch preserves the supplied path instead of removing it. The documented driver contract says an output filename forces capture, and AO already handles that rule correctly for direct reads in `images.go:110–112`. A `run_steps` request can therefore defeat screenshot opt-out/output placement and receives no adopted `Images` entry, because this method returns an empty path. A scratch service probe confirmed the outgoing arguments and a synthetic write outside the AO image root; no native batch capture was run. Delete the caller path before branching (and before early returns), then add only an AO-owned path when capture is requested. This is a screenshot-policy violation, not a claim of privilege escalation or sandboxing local callers.

[P2] Preserve elements-only accessibility reads in MCP output

On drivers exposing `tree_format:"elements"`, which AO leaves in the discovered schema, the documented response contains `elements` instead of `tree_markdown`. This renderer ignores that array but still reports success, suppressing `callCua`'s JSON fallback. With `include_screenshot:false`, a read containing real labels, tokens and frames is reduced to `window_id=9 pid=7 elements=3 snapshot_id=s1`, leaving the agent no elements to inspect or act on. A scratch probe through the unchanged renderer and `callCua` reproduced that complete loss. Render the structured array or fall back to JSON when it is the only tree representation. Contract: https://cua.ai/docs/cua-driver/reference/mcp-tools/window-state . This format-specific finding was checked against the official contract and an isolated fixture, not reproduced on the installed Linux 0.7.1 driver.

[P2] Align the batch deadline with the advertised execution budget

`run_steps` receives the same hard 45-second deadline as an ordinary call, although the driver contract advertised to agents allows a 60-second batch, up to 64 steps and `delay_ms` up to 2000. A valid 26-step batch at that delay needs 50 seconds for inter-step delays alone, so AO terminates its CLI before it can return the executed-step report/final observation. The unchanged `runCall` supplied a fake driver only 44.999994 seconds in the bounded deadline probe. Give batches their execution budget plus reporting headroom, or consistently constrain the exposed batch contract to AO's smaller limit. Contract: https://cua.ai/docs/cua-driver/reference/mcp-tools/batch-recording-and-settings . No long native batch or claim about whether daemon-side actions continue after CLI disconnection is implied; the installed Linux 0.7.1 has no `run_steps`.

Clicking submits the installer that the backend already knows it cannot run, and neither Copy command nor Install guide is available. Honor `manualCommand`/unsupported state for installed updates too, and show the reason. The component-state reproduction is isolated/mocked; the real laptop has bash, and no install/update button was clicked.

[P2] Budget artifact entries before clipping the latest turn

Without artifacts: 10,885 characters and the request is retained. With artifacts: 16,000 characters and the request is absent. Please shorten/drop artifact entries before whole-note clipping, and assert that the latest request survives at the Windows cap.

[P2] Enforce the byte budget for the added section

The added listing can exceed `handoffNoteMaxBytes` while staying below the character cap. The existing fallback calls `clipHandoffText` with only the character limit, so it returns such a note unchanged.

Each path segment fits the usual 255-byte filename limit.

Without artifacts the result is 72,445 bytes. With artifacts it is 106,240 bytes / 29,496 characters, above the 96,000-byte cap. Please budget artifact output by bytes as well as characters and add an assertion for `len(note) <= handoffNoteMaxBytes`.

[P2] Retry archive invalidation after an in-flight page finishes

Load the first archive page, start the next page, then let a poll report an increased archive count before that request finishes. This effect calls `fetchPage(key, "refresh")`, but its loading guard immediately returns. Completing the request updates `streams`, which is absent from these dependencies, so the refresh is never retried while subsequent polls report the same count. A newly archived worker above the old cursor remains missing until another count change or a manual refresh. Please queue the invalidation or recheck outstanding count changes after requests settle. Reproduced with a deferred next-page request and a summary update from 3 to 4.

[P2] Match the handback to its own launch

`partitionSubagentSteps` deliberately collects an inner launch and all its descendants under the outer launch. Here, `find(isHandback)` picks the first handback from that entire chain, so an inner agent finishing marks the still-running outer agent **Done** and displays the inner report as its report. When the outer handback arrives, the earlier handback still wins and the following filter removes both, leaving the outer report inaccessible. Executing `outer -> inner -> inner handback -> outer handback` against this implementation returns the inner report for the outer agent.

Select the handback whose `detail.parentProviderItemId` matches `launch.providerItemId`, and preserve descendant handbacks in the detail view. Please add a regression that composes partitioning with state/report derivation for nested agents.

[P2] Associate child steps across user-steer segments

`groupByTurn` calls `splitAtSteers` before rendering `TurnGroup`, so `group.items` here contains only one visual segment of the AO turn. If the user steers while a subagent is running, its launch stays in the earlier segment while later commands and its handback land in the next segment. These separate calls to `partitionSubagentSteps` cannot join them: the team never receives its report and can show **No report** while the real turn is still live, and the later child steps appear as loose parent activities.

Build the associations from the complete AO turn before splitting at steers, then carry them and the real turn's live state into the launch's segment. Cover `launch -> user steer -> child command -> handback` in the timeline integration test.

One remaining live-state edge prevents fully resolving this thread: `launch (completed background launch) -> user steer`, before any child step has arrived. `groupByTurn` returns early when `steps.size === 0` (line 5247), so the earlier segment never gets the real turn live state. `subagentsLive` falls back to false, and `readSubagent` returns `unknown`; the still-live team folds under Worked for and says No report until the first child event arrives. `withSubagentSteps` has the same omission for a launch with zero own steps when another launch does have steps.

Please carry the real live state for segments containing launches even when their step lists are empty (e.g. register each launch with an empty list). The current test already includes a child command in its first snapshot, so it misses this case.

[P2] Preserve daemon timestamp precision in archive ordering

The daemon orders `updatedAt` with nanosecond precision, but `Date.parse` truncates it to milliseconds. This makes the client comparator disagree with the order required by `mergeArchiveStreams`. For example, a non-final server page `[a@2026-10-01T00:00:00.000900Z, z@2026-10-01T00:00:00.000800Z]` incorrectly displays only `z`: the newer `a` is filtered out by the merge boundary. Other ID combinations cause later pages to insert rows above already displayed rows. Reproduced against the actual merge function.

Please compare timestamps at the same precision as the daemon and add coverage for rows within one millisecond.

Fixed in f73ed5a517. `refreshFirstPage` now reconciles the retained pages:

The deadlock can still happen here when hibernation races the relay. `Hibernate` holds the controller gate, then calls `SetSessionHibernated`, then waits up to 10s for the controller to stop. Suppose the relay reads `record` (line 2787) before the marker write. It gets `HibernatedAt == nil` and comes here. `workingController` cannot take the gate and blocks in `gate.lock`. Once hibernation releases the gate, it re-reads the record and sees `HibernatedAt != nil`. It then calls `wakeHibernated` synchronously, with the caller still holding the sessionguard input lease. The result is the same 60s stall, `resume agent ...: context deadline exceeded`, and every user send that joins the wake fails with it. The window is narrow, but it is the moment the worker goes idle, so it can overlap a CI nudge.

Suggested fix: the relay should never wake inline. For example, give `workingController` a mode (or add a relay variant) that returns a sentinel such as `errHibernated` together with the fresh record instead of calling `wakeHibernated`. Then loop back to `queueWithoutController` + `startBackgroundWake` with that record. Add a test that covers this: block hibernation between the marker write and the controller stop, start a relay that read the pre-marker record, and assert that it returns without waiting for the wake.

The window is reachable. The idle sweep, update stops and version refresh all hold an agent operation, which refuses new input leases and drains existing ones before hibernating. The relay uses `false`, so a session found asleep after the gate returns `errAsleep` instead of being woken inline, and `relayChatTurn` loops back to `queueWithoutController` + `startBackgroundWake` with a fresh read. The loop checks `ctx.Err()` each pass. Joining an in-flight wake when `HibernatedAt` is already nil is unchanged: by then the resume has drained input and holds its operation, so a leased caller cannot be waiting on it.

3. Repeat with and without the child's `stopImmediatePropagation()` call.

This PR conflicts with main (`mergeable: CONFLICTING`). Main no longer renders a single `<Markdown>` here. It splits the text into memoized `MarkdownChunk`s, and each chunk passes the module-level `PLUGINS` to `<Markdown remarkPlugins={PLUGINS} ...>` itself. When you resolve the conflict, pass the merged `plugins` down to `MarkdownChunk` as a prop (stable, so the chunk memo still holds), and use that prop in the chunk instead of `PLUGINS`. If the chunk keeps using `PLUGINS`, paths and session ids are silently not highlighted, and the tests in `ChatWorkspaceWorkerUpdates.test.tsx` should fail. Rerun them after the rebase.

This memo is keyed on the `workspaces` reference. That reference changes every time any session summary changes: the workspace query polls, and `setQueryData` patches it on session events (status, activity, PR facts). Each change creates a new plugins array, and `ChatMarkdown` passes it to `react-markdown`, so every orchestrator message and every open worker row re-parses its markdown. The `COMPONENTS` comment in `ChatMarkdown.tsx` warns against exactly this. Also, while the query has no data, `useLocalLinkSource` returns a new `[]` on every render.

Key the memo on the session set instead of the array reference. For example, build a stable string of the `id -> projectId` pairs, memoize on that string, and build the Map inside. Then the plugins change only when a session is added or removed. Ideally do this once per chat (for example in a context or a parent component), not once per `WorkerUpdateRow`. Today every row rebuilds the full Map, even when the row is collapsed.

Done in 9810f5c7bb (rebased onto main 73c01ef214). `ChatMarkdown` passes its memoized `plugins` (built-ins plus `remarkPlugins`) to every `MarkdownChunk` as a prop, and the chunk renders `<Markdown remarkPlugins={remarkPlugins} ...>` instead of `PLUGINS`. Since the array is stable, the chunk memo still holds. After the rebase I reran `ChatWorkspaceWorkerUpdates`, `session-links`, `ChatMarkdown`, `WorkerUpdates` and `streaming-markdown` (164 tests), plus `tsgo --noEmit`, and all pass. That includes the test that checks the path renders as `<code>` and the session id as an `ao://sessions/` link. GitHub now reports the PR as mergeable.

Fixed in 14797d0321. `PlainReferencesProvider` now wraps the timeline in `ChatWorkspace` and builds the plugin list once per chat. Its memo is keyed on a JSON string of the `[sessionId, projectId]` pairs, and the Map is built inside the memo. A status, activity or PR-facts patch, or the new `[]` returned while the query has no data, leaves the key unchanged, so the list keeps its identity and nothing re-parses. `OrchestratorMessage` and `WorkerUpdateRow` only read the context through `usePlainReferences()`, so collapsed rows no longer build a Map. The new test in `ChatWorkspaceWorkerUpdates.test.tsx` checks two cases: a status change keeps the list identity, and an added session gives a new list. It fails when the memo is keyed on the `workspaces` reference again. The 6 affected suites (380 tests) and `tsgo --noEmit` pass.

[P2] Honor explicit gzip rejection before selecting compression. This invokes chi v5.1.0, whose selectEncoder/matchAcceptEncoding uses strings.Contains on each comma-separated token and ignores quality values. Consequently an authenticated JSON request with Accept-Encoding: gzip;q=0 (or gzip;q=0, identity;q=1) still selects gzip and receives Content-Encoding: gzip even though the client explicitly cannot accept it. Before this change these responses were identity encoded. Please use standards-aware negotiation or guard the middleware accordingly and add q=0/mixed-preference regression cases; the current test only covers the plain gzip token. This conclusion is from the exact pinned dependency source, not an executed local reproduction.

[P2] Preserve an explicit native ephemeral prompt before reading config

If the project or inherited environment sets HERMES_EPHEMERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT, this call ignores that value and reads only config.yaml. configure then replaces the environment entry with that fallback persona plus AO's instructions. For example, Env containing HERMES_EPHEMERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT="Use my team conventions" and an empty native config produces only AO's prompt, silently losing the user's instructions. Hermes gives the environment variable precedence over config (gateway/run_config_loaders.py, _load_ephemeral_system_prompt), and GetAgentHooks already preserves this case through AO_HERMES_ORIGINAL_EPHEMERAL. Resolve the original prompt from that marker when present, otherwise from the effective native environment, and fall back to NativeEphemeralOverlay only when no explicit prompt exists. Please add coverage with an explicit env prompt as well as the config-only persona.

[P2] Preserve the rest of an MCP result when rendering images

When a Codex MCP result contains an image plus `structuredContent`, this branch replaces the entire JSON result with `ToolContent`. Its normalizer only retains `text`, `content`, and `output`, so `{content: [image], structuredContent: {answer: 42}}` now shows only the image and silently loses the answer. Embedded resource and resource-link blocks disappear for the same reason. These fields were visible through `JsonPayload` before this change, and `structuredContent` is explicitly supported by `McpToolCallResult`. Preserve the non-image result data in a sanitized text/JSON fallback alongside the images, and add a mixed-result regression test.

[P2] Preserve usage and SCM invalidations for small batches

This branch bypasses `workspaceInvalidationPending`, which was also the only local invalidation path for `sessionUsageQueryRoot` and `sessionScmSummaryQueryKey()`. Usage ingestion emits exactly an id-only `session_updated`, and reported PR outputs do the same (`0169_reported_pr_cdc.sql`). Fetching `/sessions/{id}` does not refresh either cache, and their local queries have no polling. With up to three active sessions, an open usage/cost view or PR inspector therefore stays stale until an unrelated broad event or remount. Keep those downstream invalidations, preferably scoped to the affected sessions, while avoiding the full workspace read.

[P2] Retain catch-up for events received during the loader snapshot

Opening SSE before the loader does not cover events emitted while its REST snapshot is in flight. On cold start there is no workspace observer until `ShellLayout` mounts. If `session_created` arrives after `/sessions` reads its snapshot but before the loader response settles, transport `invalidate()` checks only active in-flight queries, so it queues no catch-up; invalidating the inactive query starts no refetch, and the pending success clears the invalidation. Reusing that response here then omits the new session until a later poll/event. Track events against the inactive loader request and perform a post-settlement catch-up when needed; add a regression with CDC delivered during the initial list request.

[P2] Keep row cache writes from indefinitely postponing the workspace poll

Every successful row read calls `setQueryData` on the query that owns the 15-second workspace polling observer. TanStack Query re-arms that observer's interval on cache updates, so usage events arriving every second keep postponing the full-list poll forever. The requested head's five-minute fixture confirms this in CI: it expects 20 scheduled reads but receives zero. This removes the fallback for changes outside the patched row: for example, a project display-name update from another window/API emits no project CDC, so this window can retain the old name throughout a long agent run. Preserve a bounded full-workspace polling cadence independently of row patches and retain a regression asserting that it still runs.
Nit: an iframe's `error` event doesn't fire for HTTP or network failures, so this handler never sets `failed`. The `pageAvailable` fetch above already covers missing pages, so this could be dropped.

Nit: these Recent cards are separate instances from the same rows in Pinned and in the project section, so each one mounts its own thumbnail. For HTML that means one live scripted iframe per copy. Consider a static fallback for duplicates, or capping concurrent page previews.

[P2] Honor catalog invalidation before reusing a detached read

This map can return a pre-update catalog after an ordinary catalog CDC invalidation. If a slow OpenCode GET is pending when its last observer unmounts, TanStack cancels the query but the GET stays in this map. A subsequent `agent_model_catalog` event invalidates the now-inactive query; `event-transport.ts` schedules a catch-up only for active fetches, so it cannot see this detached request. Remounting before the GET settles then joins that old promise, publishes the pre-event catalog, and marks it fresh for ten minutes (when it has no warning). Version or discard pending entries on catalog invalidation, or ensure a post-invalidation read follows a reused request. Add coverage for a catalog event between unmount and remount; the login test explicitly clears the map and does not cover this path.

[P2] Refresh the conversation after a failed wake

A failed wake does not guarantee the completion event assumed above. The daemon clears HibernatedAt before resuming the provider, so its CDC event can refresh the conversation while isWaking is still true and cache a hibernated snapshot. If native resume subsequently fails (for example, a Codex thread/resume timeout), wakeHibernated.finish only clears in-memory state and emits no further event. Swallowing this rejection removes the previous failure refresh; local conversations have staleTime: Infinity, so the stopped-controller banner and Resume agent action remain hidden until an unrelated refresh. Preserve a targeted conversation refresh after wake failure, or guarantee a completion event, and cover the clear-marker event arriving before the failed resume.

[P2] Preserve paragraph separators when copying formulas

The global `copy-tex` handler replaces clipboard plain text with `katexReplaceWithTex(fragment).textContent`. [P2] Refresh repair metadata when a single block changes dialect

A single block still has dialect-dependent `repairInline` metadata. If a reply is streaming `$a~b$` with math off, enabling math while no new text arrives takes this shortcut and retains `repairInline: true`. `MarkdownChunk` therefore feeds remend's altered `$a\~b$` to KaTeX instead of the original formula; a fresh math parse would disable repair. [P2] Reserve v1 before checking its Homebrew link

Homebrew's reinstall flow temporarily removes v1's linked marker before acquiring installation locks. Planning v2 during that interval leaves `alsoChanges` empty, allowing v2 commands to run despite v1's locked gate and active job; a focused regression reproduced this bypass. Source tracing indicates backup restoration can then race v2's linking and cleanup, leaving the default executable unavailable. Always reserve v1 first, then inspect its linked state. See the [Homebrew reinstall flow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/brew/main/Library/Homebrew/reinstall/reinstall.rb).

[P2] Finish restoration before normal shutdown exits

Each cleanup command can run for two minutes, but daemon shutdown drains installers for only ten seconds before continuing its exit (`daemon.go:1179-1183`). Quitting while the v2 unlink stalls can therefore terminate the daemon before `brew link opencode` runs, leaving v1 unavailable on PATH. Startup recovery does not restore the link. A scaled regression reproduced the incomplete restoration. Align cleanup with shutdown draining, or persist and recover unfinished restoration.

**[P2] Record requirements against the model that ran the turn**

The selected model is mutable while a turn is running. Reproduced through the actual ACP fake-agent flow:

1. Start and block a prompt on model A.
2. Successfully call `SetConfigOption("model", "model-B")` while A is running.
3. Release A's response.
4. Observe this failure callback receive `"model-B"`.

For a version rejection, `claudeVersionTooOldFailure` then persists A's minimum version against B, disabling a supported model across restarts while leaving A unlearned. `reportServedModel` has the same mutable-selection problem and can attribute A's transcript output to a newly selected alias. Capture the model used by the turn and pass that value to both hooks.

**[P2] Automatic selection still chooses gated models**

Clearing `IsDefault` does not prevent automatic selection: `foldClaudeAliasDefault` restores the flag on the newest model, and `TaskComposer`'s newest-Opus fallback ignores `unavailableReason` independently of that flag. A fresh-composer reproduction submitted `model: "claude-opus-5-5"` without any model selection despite the disabled row, so the new spawn check rejects the default task with `UNSUPPORTED_MODEL`. **[P2] Running chats bypass the picker gate**

Propagate availability into the running-chat choices and enforce it when changing models.

**[P2] Apply the gate to revalidation responses**

`Models` and `ModelCatalog` now apply the gate, but `RevalidateModels` still returns only `withModelUsage`. Routine picker revalidation calls `POST /models/refresh?revalidate=true`, then replaces the shared catalog with this raw response, re-enabling unsupported models and restoring their default flags. A focused reproduction returned `requiresVersion: "9.9.9"` from `Models` and empty availability fields from the immediately following `RevalidateModels` call. Apply `gateModels` to that return path too, while keeping the durable cache raw.

**[P2] Local CLI versions incorrectly disable cloud choices**

Cloud task creation consumes the local daemon's Claude catalog too: `TaskComposer` uses the local query for Claude even when `isCloudProject` is true, then passes these availability fields to `AgentModelCombobox`. With local Claude `2.1.239`, the cloud picker disables Opus 5.5 although cloud workers run `2.1.287` (`workerexec.ClaudeCodeVersion`) and satisfy its `2.1.280` requirement. A cloud-composer reproduction confirmed the model is rendered with `aria-disabled="true"`. Use the worker's version for cloud availability, or omit the local version restrictions from cloud choices.

**[P1] Persist the TUI stop before enabling idle updates on Unix.**

For an idle, resumable TUI session, the real `StopHarnessSessions` destroys the runtime but leaves `Activity=idle` and `HibernatedAt=nil` in the session store (`session_manager/update_when_idle.go:184-206`). The immediate `harnessInUse` recheck in `runIdleBatch` therefore still counts that session as live, aborts the install, resumes the old release, and can repeat this every 10 seconds. This newly affects Unix harnesses routed through the idle flow, including Muse. A regression using the real session manager reproduced `activity=idle hibernated=<nil> destroyed=1` after a successful stop; the existing coordinator stub hides the mismatch by setting `HibernatedAt` for every stopped fixture. Persist a conclusively stopped controller fact without terminating the session before returning from `StopHarnessSessions`, and cover the full TUI stop/update/resume path.

**[P2] Register release sources for the new official recipes.**

`officialSourceFor` still has no `TargetQwen`, `TargetMemcode`, or `TargetOpencodeV2` entry. Their official installs consequently return an advisory with `status=unknown`, `reason=unsupported_source`, and no latest version, so the update notice cannot offer these managed recipes. Register their release feeds and add advisory tests for official installs instead of only seeding a ready-made advisory.

After a Codex cask update creates an AO-managed release, `planForOperation` clears `plan.Script` before checking managed reinstall eligibility (`agentplans.go:372-375`). This new requirement for a non-nil script rejects that managed plan, so Reinstall falls through to `brew reinstall --cask codex` while AO continues selecting its own managed launcher. A damaged managed copy remains unrepaired. A planner regression reproduced `managed=false`, `script=nil`, and `brew reinstall --cask codex` for a managed Codex record. Build a managed reinstall plan using the official recipe and pin it to `managedRecord.Version`.

The isolated environment preserves `SHELL`, but `runOfficialManagedInstall` creates only `.install-home`. With `SHELL` pointing to fish, [fx's installer](https://fx.sh/setup.sh) appends its PATH line to `$HOME/.config/fish/config.fish` without creating that parent directory. Reproduced offline with Bash 5.3.3: the script installs the fixture binary, then exits 1 on the missing profile path, so AO treats the update as failed and removes the new release. Set a neutral `SHELL` for the recipe or create the required private profile directory, and cover a fish environment.

The one-slash branch allows exactly one dot in the filename, so common paths such as `src/App.test.tsx`, `src/index.d.ts`, and `config/.env.local` match neither path expression. [P2] Use zlib framing for negotiated deflate

A request with `Accept-Encoding: deflate` or `gzip;q=0, deflate;q=1` now selects deflate, but [chi v5.1.0's encoderDeflate](https://github.com/go-chi/chi/blob/v5.1.0/middleware/compress.go) uses `compress/flate.NewWriter` and emits raw DEFLATE. Correction to my earlier reply. Reopening this thread because the finding is only partly addressed at `03234191191b31ef9320ba9e118ed126110cd754`.

The residual is not equivalent to TanStack's baseline deduplication. TanStack 5.101.0 dispatches `invalidate` only when the query is not already invalidated, and a failed read sets that flag with no event. In both states a catalog CDC event cannot discard a pending OpenCode read:

1. An invalidated picker mounts and starts GET2.
2. CDC arrives during GET2. The transport marks a catch-up because the fetch is active, but `invalidate()` is a no-op, so no event fires.
3. The picker unmounts. The revert restores `isInvalidated` and settles CDC's `invalidateQueries`, so the catch-up fires now and is also a no-op.
4. The picker remounts before GET2 settles and reuses GET2.
5. GET2's pre-event catalog is published, saved to the snapshot and marked fresh. It stays until the next catalog event or the 10-minute stale time. With refresh-in-progress state it self-heals in about 3 s.

After a failed read, a single CDC event between unmount and remount is enough. `main` has no pending map, so it issues a post-event read in the same sequence.

```
remote: Permission to Pritom14/Assignment11.3.git denied to aoagentsdev123[bot].
fatal: unable to access 'https://staging-api.aoagents.dev/api/cloud/v1/worker/git/<session>/Pritom14/Assignment11.3.git/': The requested URL returned error: 403
```

I ruled out the code path: the same `proxyWriteToken` run locally against the same installation (166930545) and repository (80397559) returns a token that gets 200 on `info/refs?service=git-receive-pack`, and a `contents:read` token reproduces the 403 exactly. So it looks like GitHub briefly not honouring a just-minted write token on the git frontend. The old design hid this because each credential-helper call minted again and git retried.

Example fix: retry only the ref advertisement (a GET with no body, so it is safe to replay) on 403 for a push, with a short backoff:

```go
response, err := s.gitProxyClient.Do(upstream)
for attempt := 1; err == nil && request.push && r.Method == http.MethodGet &&
	response.StatusCode == http.StatusForbidden && attempt <= 4; attempt++ {
	response.Body.Close()
	select {
	case <-time.After(time.Duration(attempt) * 2 * time.Second): // 2, 4, 6, 8 s
	case <-ctx.Done():
		return
	}
	s.logger.Info("git proxy retrying a refused push advertisement", "repository", request.owner+"/"+request.repo, "attempt", attempt)
	response, err = s.gitProxyClient.Do(upstream.Clone(ctx))
}
```

The POST cannot be replayed (the pack is streamed), but once `info/refs` succeeds the token is usable, so retrying the advertisement covers it. Worth a test with an upstream that answers 403 twice and then 200.
